occurrences.alt: This illustration shows two silhouettes of a human female, each showing the components of a different organ system. The integumentary system encloses internal body structures and is the site of many sensory receptors. The integumentary system includes the hair, skin, and nails. The skeletal system supports the body and, along with the muscular system, enables movement. The skeletal system includes cartilage, such as that at the tip of the nose, as well as the bones and joints.

This illustration shows two silhouettes of a human female, each showing the components of a different organ system.
The muscular system enables movement, along with the skeletal system, but also helps to maintain body temperature. The muscular system includes skeletal muscles, as well as tendons that connect skeletal muscles to bones. The nervous system detects and processes sensory information and activates bodily responses. The nervous system includes the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, such as those located in the limbs.

This illustration shows two silhouettes of a human female, each showing the components of a different organ system.
The endocrine system secretes hormones and regulates bodily processes. The endocrine system includes the pituitary gland in the brain, the thyroid gland in the throat, the pancreas in the abdomen, the adrenal glands on top of the kidneys, and the testes in the scrotum of males as well as the ovaries in the pelvic region of females. The cardiovascular system delivers oxygen and nutrients to the tissues as well as equalizes temperature in the body. The cardiovascular system includes the heart and blood vessels.

occurrences.alt: This illustration shows biological organization as a pyramid. The chemical level is at the apex of the pyramid where atoms bond to form molecules with three dimensional structures. An example is shown with two white hydrogen atoms bonding to a red oxygen atom to create water. The next level down on the pyramid is the cellular level, as illustrated with a long, tapered, smooth muscle cell. At this level, a variety of molecules combine to form the interior fluid and organelles of a body cell. The next level down is the tissue level. A community of similar cells forms body tissue. The example given here is a section of smooth muscle tissue, which contains many smooth muscle cells closely bound side by side. The next level down is the organ level, as illustrated with the bladder and urethra. The bladder contains smooth muscle while the urethra contains skeletal muscle. These are both examples of muscle tissues. The next level down is the organ system level, as illustrated by the entire urinary system containing the kidney, ureters, bladder and urethra. At this level, two or more organs work closely together to perform the functions of a body system. At the base of the pyramid is the organismal level illustrated with a woman drinking water. At this level, many organ systems work harmoniously together to perform the functions of an independent organism.
occurrences.slide_text:
Levels of Structural Organization of the Human Body
The organization of the body often is discussed in terms of six distinct levels of increasing complexity, from the smallest chemical building blocks to a unique human organism.
AtomsMoleculesOrganellesCellsTissueOrganOrgan systemsOrganism

occurrences.alt: This figure shows two flow charts labeled A and B. Chart A shows a general negative feedback loop. The loop starts with a stimulus. Information about the stimulus is perceived by a sensor which sends that information to a control center. The control center sends a signal to an effector, which creates a response. That then feeds back to the top of the flow chart by inhibiting the stimulus. Part B shows body temperature regulation as an example of negative feedback system. Here, the stimulus is body temperature exceeding 37 degrees Celsius. The sensor is a set of nerve cells in the skin and brain and the control center is the temperature regulatory center of the brain. The effectors are sweat glands throughout the body which lead to increased heat loss and inhibit the rising body temperature.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the steps of a positive feedback loop as a series of stepwise arrows looping around a diagram of an infant within the uterus of a pregnant woman. Initially the head of the baby pushes against the cervix, transmitting nerve impulses from the cervix to the brain. Next the brain stimulates the pituitary gland to secrete oxytocin which is carried in the bloodstream to the uterus. Finally, the oxytocin simulates uterine contractions and pushes the baby harder into the cervix. As the head of the baby pushes against the cervix with greater and greater force, the uterine contractions grow stronger and more frequent. This mechanism is a positive feedback loop.

Anterior (or ventral): Describes the front or direction toward the front of the body. The toes are anterior to the foot.

Superior (or cranial) describes a position above or higher than another part of the body proper. The orbits are superior to the oris.
Inferior (or caudal) describes a position below or lower than another part of the body proper; near or toward the tail (in humans, the coccyx, or lowest part of the spinal column). The pelvis is inferior to the abdomen.

occurrences.alt: This illustration shows a female viewed from her right, front side. The anatomical planes are depicted as blue rectangles passing through the woman’s body. The frontal or coronal plane enters through the right side of the body, passes through the body, and exits from the left side. It divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) halves. The sagittal plane enters through the back and emerges through the front of the body. It divides the body into right and left halves. The transverse plane passes through the body perpendicular to the frontal and sagittal planes. This plane is a cross section which divides the body into upper and lower halves.
occurrences.slide_text:
Sagittal plane
Divides the body or an organ vertically into right and left sides.
If it runs directly down the middle of the body and gives equal left and right parts, it is called the midsagittal or median plane. 
If it gives unequal left and right parts, it is called parasagittal plane.

Frontal (coronal) plane
Divides the body or an organ into an anterior (front) portion and a posterior (rear) portion. The frontal plane is often referred to as a coronal plane. (“Corona” is Latin for “crown.”)

The transverse plane is the plane that divides the body or organ horizontally into upper and lower portions. 
Transverse planes produce images referred to as cross sections.

occurrences.alt: This illustration shows a lateral and anterior view of the body and highlights the body cavities with different colors. The cranial cavity is a large, bean-shaped cavity filling most of the upper skull where the brain is located. The vertebral cavity is a very narrow, thread-like cavity running from the cranial cavity down the entire length of the spinal cord. Together the cranial cavity and vertebral cavity can be referred to as the dorsal body cavity. The thoracic cavity consists of three cavities that fill the interior area of the chest. The two pleural cavities are situated on both sides of the body, anterior to the spine and lateral to the breastbone. The superior mediastinum is a wedge-shaped cavity located between the superior regions of the two thoracic cavities. The pericardial cavity within the mediastinum is located at the center of the chest below the superior mediastinum. The pericardial cavity roughly outlines the shape of the heart. The diaphragm divides the thoracic and the abdominal cavities. The abdominal cavity occupies the entire lower half of the trunk, anterior to the spine. Just under the abdominal cavity, anterior to the buttocks, is the pelvic cavity. The pelvic cavity is funnel shaped and is located inferior and anterior to the abdominal cavity. Together the abdominal and pelvic cavity can be referred to as the abdominopelvic cavity while the thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic cavities together can be referred to as the ventral body cavity.

This illustration shows two silhouettes of a human female, each showing the components of a different organ system.
The lymphatic system returns fluid to the blood and defends against pathogens. The lymphatic system includes the thymus in the chest, the spleen in the abdomen, the lymphatic vessels that spread throughout the body, and the lymph nodes distributed along the lymphatic vessels. The respiratory system removes carbon dioxide from the body and delivers oxygen to the blood. The respiratory system includes the nasal passages, the trachea, and the lungs.

The digestive system includes the stomach, the liver, the gall bladder (connected to the liver), the large intestine, and the small intestine. The urinary system controls water balance in the body and removes and excretes waste from the blood. The urinary system includes the kidneys and the urinary bladder. The reproductive system of males and females produce sex hormones and gametes. The male reproductive system is specialized to deliver gametes to the female while the female reproductive system is specialized to support the embryo and fetus until birth and produce milk for the infant after birth. The male reproductive system includes the two testes within the scrotum as well as the epididymis which wraps around each testis. The female reproductive system includes the mammary glands within the breasts and the ovaries and uterus within the pelvic cavity.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the pericardium on the left next to an analogy of a hand punching a balloon on the right. The pericardium is a two-layered sac that surrounds the entire heart except where the blood vessels emerge on the heart’s superior side. The pericardium has two layers because it folds over itself in the shape of the letter U. The inner layer that borders the heart is the visceral pericardium while the outer layer is the parietal pericardium. The space between the two layers is called the pericardial cavity. The heart sits in the cavity much like a fist punching into a balloon. The balloon surrounds the lower part of the fist with a two-layered sac, with the top of the balloon, where it contacts the fist, being analogous to the visceral pericardium. The bottom of the balloon, where it is tied off, is analogous to the parietal pericardium. The air within the balloon is analogous to the pericardial cavity.

occurrences.alt: This illustration has two parts. Part A shows the abdominopelvic regions. These regions divide the abdomen into nine squares. The upper right square is the right hypochondriac region and contains the base of the right ribs. The upper left square is the left hypochondriac region and contains the base of the left ribs. The epigastric region is the upper central square and contains the bottom edge of the liver as well as the upper areas of the stomach. The diaphragm curves like an upside down U over these three regions. The central right region is called the right lumbar region and contains the ascending colon and the right edge of the small intestines. The central square contains the transverse colon and the upper regions of the small intestines. The left lumbar region contains the left edge of the transverse colon and the left edge of the small intestine. The lower right square is the right iliac region and contains the right pelvic bones and the ascending colon. The lower left square is the left iliac region and contains the left pelvic bone and the lower left regions of the small intestine. The lower central square contains the bottom of the pubic bones, upper regions of the bladder and the lower region of the small intestine. Part B shows four abdominopelvic quadrants. The right upper quadrant (RUQ) includes the lower right ribs, right side of the liver, and right side of the transverse colon. The left upper quadrant (LUQ) includes the lower left ribs, stomach, and upper left area of the transverse colon. The right lower quadrant (RLQ) includes the right half of the small intestines, ascending colon, right pelvic bone and upper right area of the bladder. The left lower quadrant (LLQ) contains the left half of the small intestine and left pelvic bone.

occurrences.alt: This illustration shows an anterior and posterior view of the human body. The cranial region encompasses the upper part of the head while the facial region encompasses the lower half of the head beginning below the ears. The eyes are referred to as the ocular region. The cheeks are referred to as the buccal region. The ears are referred to as the auricle or otic region. The nose is referred to as the nasal region. The chin is referred to as the mental region. The neck is referred to as the cervical region. The trunk of the body contains, from superior to inferior, the thoracic region encompassing the chest, the mammary region encompassing each breast, the abdominal region encompassing the stomach area, the coxal region encompassing the belt line, and the pubic region encompassing the area above the genitals. The umbilicus, or naval, is located at the center of the abdomen. The pelvis and legs contain, from superior to inferior, the inguinal or groin region between the legs and the genitals, the pubic region surrounding the genitals, the femoral region encompassing the thighs, the patellar region encompassing the knee, the crural region encompassing the lower leg, the tarsal region encompassing the ankle, the pedal region encompassing the foot and the digital/phalangeal region encompassing the toes. The great toe is referred to as the hallux. The regions of the upper limbs, from superior to inferior, are the axillary region encompassing the armpit, the brachial region encompassing the upper arm, the antecubital region encompassing the front of the elbow, the antebrachial region encompassing the forearm, the carpal region encompassing the wrist, the palmar region encompassing the palm, and the digital/phalangeal region encompassing the fingers. The thumb is referred to as the pollux. The posterior view contains, from superior to inferior, the cervical region encompassing the neck, the dorsal region encompassing the upper back and the lumbar region encompassing the lower back. The regions of the back of the arms, from superior to inferior, include the cervical region encompassing the neck, acromial region encompassing the shoulder, the brachial region encompassing the upper arm, the olecranal region encompassing the back of the elbow, the antebrachial region encompasses the back of the arm, and the manual region encompassing the palm of the hand. The posterior regions of the legs, from superior to inferior, include the gluteal region encompassing the buttocks, the femoral region encompassing the thigh, the popliteus region encompassing the back of the knee, the sural region encompassing the back of the lower leg, and the plantar region encompassing the sole of the foot. Some regions are combined into larger regions. These include the trunk, which is a combination of the thoracic, mammary, abdominal, naval, and coxal regions. The cephalic region is a combination of all of the head regions. The upper limb region is a combination of all of the arm regions. The lower limb region is a combination of all of the leg regions.

occurrences.slide_text:
Action Potentials in Cardiac Contractile Cells
There is a rapid depolarization, followed by a plateau phase and then repolarization. 
This phenomenon accounts for the long refractory periods required for the cardiac muscle cells to pump blood effectively before they are capable of firing for a second time.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
Steps of AP in Cardiac Contractile Cells-1
Voltage-gated channels rapidly open, beginning depolarization. 
Membrane potential reaches to approximately +30 mV, at which point the sodium channels close. 
Depolarization period is very rapid and short (lasts 3–5 ms).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel of this figure shows millivolts as a function of time with the various stages labeled. It shows the action potential in the heart muscles.
occurrences.slide_text:
Steps of AP in Cardiac Contractile Cells-2
The plateau phase: membrane potential declines relatively slowly. 
This is due in large part to the opening of the slow Ca2+ channels, allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell while few K+ channels are open, allowing K+ to exit the cell. 
The relatively long plateau phase lasts approximately 175 ms.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the action potential and tension as a function of time for cardiac muscle.
occurrences.slide_text:
Steps of AP in Cardiac Contractile Cells-3
The plateau will sustain contraction for longer period of time.
This is needed to ensure powerful contractions to empty the ventricles and push the blood through Aorta and other part of the systemic circuit.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The bottom left panel shows action potential and tension as a function of time for skeletal muscle, and the bottom right panel shows the action potential and tension as a function of time for cardiac muscle.
occurrences.slide_text:
Steps of AP in Cardiac Contractile Cells-4
Once the membrane potential reaches approximately zero, the Ca2+ channels close and K+ channels open, allowing K+ to exit the cell. 
The repolarization lasts approximately 75 ms. 
At this point, membrane potential drops until it reaches resting levels once more and the cycle repeats. 
The entire event lasts between 250 and 300 ms
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The bottom left panel shows action potential and tension as a function of time for skeletal muscle, and the bottom right panel shows the action potential and tension as a function of time for cardiac muscle.
occurrences.slide_text:
Steps of AP in Cardiac Contractile Cells-5
The absolute refractory period for cardiac contractile muscle lasts approximately 200 ms, and the relative refractory period lasts approximately 50 ms
Without extended refractory periods, premature or weak  contractions would occur and lead to insufficient blood supplies.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows action potential and tension as a function of time for skeletal muscle, and the right panel shows the action potential and tension as a function of time for cardiac muscle.
occurrences.slide_text:
Skeletal vs Cardiac Contractile Cells
AP in skeletal muscles is short (1-2 ms), in cardiac it is longer (200 ms)
Contraction in skeletal muscles last 15-100, whereas it lasts 250-300 ms in cardiac cells.

occurrences.alt: These two diagrams each show a channel protein embedded in the cell membrane. In the left diagram, there is a large number of sodium ions (NA plus) and calcium ions (CA two plus) in the extracellular fluid. Within the cytosol, there is a large number of potassium ions (K plus) but only a few sodium ions. In this diagram, the channel is closed. Two ACH molecules are floating in the extracellular fluid. Their label indicates that a neurotransmitter, a ligand, is required to open the ion channel. The neurotransmitter receptor site on the extracellular fluid side of the channel protein matches the shape of the ACH molecules. In the right diagram, the two ACH molecules attach to the neurotransmitter receptor sites on the channel protein. This opens the channel and the sodium and calcium ions diffuse through the channel and into the cytosol, down their concentration gradient. The potassium ions also diffuse through the channel in the opposite direction down their concentration gradient (out of the cell and into the extracellular fluid).
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Membrane Potentials
A ligand-gated channel opens because a signaling molecule, a ligand, binds to the extracellular region of the channel.

occurrences.slide_text:
1-CNS Control of ANS
The hypothalamus is the control center for many homeostatic mechanisms. It regulates both autonomic function and endocrine function.
It receives input from cerebral structures and projects to brain stem and spinal cord structures to regulate the balance of sympathetic and parasympathetic input to the organ systems of the body. 
The main pathways for this are the medial forebrain bundle and the dorsal longitudinal fasciculus

occurrences.alt: This illustration shows the anatomy of a neuron. The neuron has a very irregular cell body (soma) containing a purple nucleus. There are six projections protruding from the top, bottom and left side of the cell body. Each of the projections branches many times, forming small, tree-shaped structures protruding from the cell body. The right side of the cell body tapers into a long cord called the axon. The axon is insulated by segments of myelin sheath, which resemble a semitransparent toilet paper roll wound around the axon. The myelin sheath is not continuous, but is separated into equally spaced segments. The bare axon segments between the sheath segments are called nodes of Ranvier. An oligodendrocyte is reaching its two arm like projections onto two myelin sheath segments. The axon branches many times at its end, where it connects to the dendrites of another neuron. Each connection between an axon branch and a dendrite is called a synapse. The cell membrane completely surrounds the cell body, dendrites, and its axon. The axon of another nerve is seen in the upper left of the diagram connecting with the dendrites of the central neuron.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Neuron
They are responsible for the electrical signals that communicate information about sensations, and that produce movements in response to those stimuli, along with inducing thought processes within the brain.

Axon hillock: where the axon emerges from the cell body.

occurrences.slide_text:
2-CNS Control of ANS
The amygdala is a group of nuclei in the medial region of the temporal lobe that is part of the limbic lobe.
The limbic lobe involved in emotional responses, and contribute to memory function. 
Limbic lobe has strong connections with the hypothalamus and influences the state of its activity on the basis of emotional state. 
For example, when you are anxious or scared, the amygdala will send signals to the hypothalamus that will stimulate the sympathetic fight-or-flight response.

occurrences.slide_text:
Autonomic Innervation of the Heart-1
Nervous control over HR is centralized within the two cardiovascular centers of the medulla oblongata
The cardioaccelerator regions stimulate activity via sympathetic stimulation of the cardioaccelerator nerves to both the SA and AV nodes, plus additional fibers to the atria and ventricles.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the brain and the nerves connecting the brain to the heart.
occurrences.slide_text:
Autonomic Innervation of the Heart-2
The cardioinhibitory centers decrease heart activity via parasympathetic stimulation of the vagus nerve. The vagus nerve sends branches to both the SA and AV nodes, and to portions of both the atria and ventricles.
During rest, both centers stimulate the heart, contributing to autonomic tone. 
Normally, vagal stimulation predominates. If left unregulated, the SA node would initiate a sinus rhythm of approximately 100 bpm. At rest the heart beats at 60-100 bpm.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the later steps of Figure 12.13. A hand is placed under flowing water. The axon of a motor neuron travels down the forearm and then branches as it reaches the hand. Each branch synapses with a different skeletal muscle in the hand. The synapse between the axon branches and the muscle is a neuromuscular junction. An impulse travelling down the motor neuron will cause the skeletal muscles to contract, resulting in muscle movement. In this case, the movement results in the person adjusting the faucet dials to change the temperature of the water.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Function of Nervous Tissue
Three components:
Integration: the signal ends in CNS where it is handled by special centers that analyze the data and make a decision about it. In this example: to open the hot water facet.

occurrences.alt: The graph has membrane potential, in millivolts, on the X axis, ranging from negative 90 to positive 30. Time is on the X axis. The left half of the plot line is labeled the depolarizing graded potential. The plot has four progressively larger peaks, with each starting at the resting membrane potential of negative 70. The lowest peak reaches to about negative 65 and is narrow in width, as this represents a small stimulus that causes a small depolarization of the cell membrane. The second peak reaches to about negative 60 but is still narrow. This represents a larger stimulus causing more depolarization. The third peak also reaches to negative 60, but is about twice as wide as the other two peaks. This represents a stimulus of longer duration, which causes a longer lasting depolarization. However, this stimulus is not greater in strength than the previous stimulus. The rightmost peak among the depolarizing graded potentials reaches above the threshold line to about negative 51. This represents a stimulus of sufficient strength to trigger an action potential. The right half of the plot is labeled the hyperpolarizing graded potential. The plot line in this half begins at the resting potential of negative 70, but then drops to more negative membrane potentials. The first peak drops to negative 75 EV, the second peak drops to negative 80 EV and the third peak drops to negative 88 EV. These peaks represent a stimulus that results in hyperpolarization, which is triggered by the activation of specific ion channels in the cell membrane.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows several types of nervous system cells associated with two multipolar neurons. Astrocytes are star shaped-cells with many dendrite like projections but no axon. They are connected with the multipolar neurons and other cells in the diagram through their dendrite like projections. Ependymal cells have a teardrop shaped cell body and a long tail that branches several times before connecting with astrocytes and the multipolar neuron. Microglial cells are small cells with rectangular bodies and many dendrite like projections stemming from their shorter sides. The projections are so extensive that they give the microglial cell a fuzzy appearance. The oligodendrocytes have circular cell bodies with four dendrite like projections. Each projection is connected to a segment of myelin sheath on the axons of the multipolar neurons. The oligodendrocytes are the same color as the myelin sheath segment and are adding layers to the sheath using their projections.

occurrences.slide_text:
Conduction System of the Heart-3
 Sinoatrial (SA) Node
Establishes the normal cardiac rhythm
Located in the superior and posterior walls of the right atrium 
Has the highest inherent rate of depolarization and is known as the pacemaker of the heart 100/minute. 
It initiates the sinus rhythm, or normal electrical pattern followed by contraction of the heart.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the anterior view of the frontal section of the heart with the major parts labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Conduction System of the Heart-4
 Atrioventricular (AV) Node
Located in the inferior portion of the right atrium within the atrioventricular septum. 
The small diameter of the cells of the node delays impulses transmission. Signals take100 ms to pass through the node.
This allows the atria to contract at the same time and complete their contraction before the impulse is transmitted to the ventricles.
Has an inherent rate of 50×/minute in absence of SA node input

Conduction System of the Heart-5
Atrioventricular Bundle (Bundle of His)
Proceeds through the interventricular septum.
Connects the atria to ventricles electrically. 
Bundle Branches
commonly called the left and right bundle branches. 
The left bundle branch supplies the left ventricle, and the right bundle branch the right ventricle. 
Carry the signals toward the apex of the heart.

Conduction System of the Heart-6
The Purkinje fibers 
Extend throughout the myocardium from the apex of the heart toward the atrioventricular septum and the base of the heart. 
Since the electrical stimulus begins at the apex, the contraction also begins at the apex and travels toward the base of the heart. 
This allows the blood to be pumped out of the ventricles and into the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

occurrences.alt: This illustration shows a cross section of skin tissue. The outermost layer is called the epidermis, and occupies one fifth of the cross section. Several hairs are emerging from the surface. The epidermis dives around one of the hairs, forming a follicle. The middle layer is called the dermis, which occupies four fifths of the cross section. The dermis contains an erector pilli muscle connected to one of the follicles. The dermis also contains an eccrine sweat gland, composed of a bunch of tubules. One tubule travels up from the bunch, through the epidermis, opening onto the surface a pore. There are two string-like nerves travelling vertically through the dermis. The right nerve is attached to a Pacinian corpuscle, which is a yellow structure consisting of concentric ovals similar to an onion. The lowest level of the skin, the hypodermis, contains fatty tissue, arteries, and veins. Blood vessels travel from the hypodermis and connect to hair follicles and erector pilli muscle in the dermis.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows a cross section of the skin containing a hair follicle. The follicle is teardrop shaped. Its enlarged base, labeled the hair bulb, is embedded in the hypodermis. The outermost layer of the follicle is the epidermis, which invaginates from the skin surface to envelope the follicle. Within the epidermis is the outer root sheath, which is only present on the hair bulb. It does not extend up the shaft of the hair. Within the outer root sheath is the inner root sheath. The inner root sheath extends about half of the way up the hair shaft, ending midway through the dermis. The hair matrix is the innermost layer. The hair matrix surrounds the bottom of the hair shaft where it is embedded within the hair bulb. The hair shaft, in itself, contains three layers: the outermost cuticle, a middle layer called the cortex, and an innermost layer called the medulla.

Hair
Primarily made of dead, keratinized cells.
Strands of hair originate in an epidermal penetration of the dermis called the hair follicle.
The hair shaft is the part of the hair not anchored to the follicle, and much of this is exposed at the skin’s surface.

Structure of a Hair 
The rest of the hair, which is anchored in the follicle, lies below the surface of the skin and is referred to as the hair root. 
The hair root ends deep in the dermis at the hair bulb, and includes a layer of mitotically active basal cells called the hair matrix. 
The hair bulb surrounds the hair papilla, which is made of connective tissue and contains blood capillaries and nerve endings from the dermis

Functions of a Hair 
Hair serves a variety of functions, including protection, sensory input, thermoregulation, and communication.

Structure of a Hair Follicle
Each hair root is connected to a smooth muscle called the arrector pili that contracts in response to nerve signals from the sympathetic nervous system, making the external hair shaft “stand up” to trap a layer of air to add insulation.
This will close the openings of the sweat pores.

1-Sebaceous Gland
A type of oil gland that is found all over the body and helps to lubricate and waterproof the skin and hair. 
Most sebaceous glands are associated with hair follicles. They generate and excrete sebum, a mixture of lipids, onto the skin surface, thereby naturally lubricating cells of the stratum corneum, keeping it flexible.

2-Sebaceous Gland
The fatty acids of sebum also have antibacterial properties, and prevent water loss from the skin in low-humidity environments. 
The secretion of sebum is stimulated by hormones, many of which do not become active until puberty. Thus, sebaceous glands are relatively inactive during childhood.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the left adrenal gland located atop the left kidney. The gland is composed of an outer cortex and an inner medulla all surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. The cortex can be subdivided into additional zones, all of which produce different types of hormones. The outermost layer is the zona glomerulosa, which releases mineralcorticoids, such as aldosterone, that regulate mineral balance. Underneath this layer is the zona fasciculate, which releases glucocorticoids, such as cortisol, corticosterone and cortisone, that regulate glucose metabolism. Underneath this layer is the zona reticularis, which releases androgens, such as dehydroepiandrosterone, that stimulate masculinization. Below this layer is the adrenal medulla, which releases stress hormones, such as epinephrine and norepinephrine, that stimulate the sympathetic ANS.

occurrences.slide_text:
Cardiac Cycle-2
The cardiac cycle begins with atrial systole and progresses to
ventricular systole, atrial diastole, and ventricular diastole, when the cycle begins again.
Can be divide into 3 major steps:
Isovolumic relaxation
Ventricular filling
Ventricular systole
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This pie chart shows the different phases of the cardiac cycle and details the atrial and ventricular stages.
occurrences.slide_text:
Cardiac Cycle-3
Ventricular filling
Both atria and ventricle in diastole.
Blood passively flow to atria. Blood pressure will open AV valves and blood will flow to ventricles. 
P wave occurs and initiate atrial contraction (systole) to force the remaining of blood into ventricles. 
At the same time ventricles start to depolarize (QRS complex)

occurrences.alt: This pie chart shows the different phases of the cardiac cycle and details the atrial and ventricular stages.
occurrences.slide_text:
Cardiac Cycle-4
Ventricular Systole-A
Atria in diastole and relaxed, almost empty. 
Ventricles depolarized and starting systole.
AV valves closed and no enough pressure to open the SL valves. This sub-phase is called the isovolumetric contraction phase.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This pie chart shows the different phases of the cardiac cycle and details the atrial and ventricular stages.
occurrences.slide_text:
Cardiac Cycle-5
Ventricular Systole-B 
The sustained contraction of the ventricles will increase blood pressure and exceed that in arteries (mainly Aorta) which will open the SL valves. 
Blood will leave the ventricles. This sub-phase is called the ejection phase. 
Some blood will remain in ventricles. This is called the End Systolic Volume (ESV)
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This pie chart shows the different phases of the cardiac cycle and details the atrial and ventricular stages.
occurrences.slide_text:
Cardiac Cycle-6
Isovolumic relaxation 
Atria and ventricles in diastole 
Ventricles repolarized relaxed, and empty expect ESV.
Atria repolarized, repolarized and passively being filled with blood (AV valves are closed).
SL valves are closed due to blood backflow. 
When blood pressure in atria opens the AV valves, the cycle starts again

occurrences.slide_text:
Eccrine (Merocrine) Sweat Glands
Produces sweat for thermoregulation.
These glands are found all over the skin’s surface, but are especially abundant on the palms of the hand, the soles of the feet, and the forehead
The duct rising up to a pore on the skin surface
Function: a primary component of thermoregulation in humans and thus help to maintain homeostasis.

The pituitary gland looks like a sac containing two balls hanging from the infundibulum. The “balls” are the anterior and posterior lobes of the pituitary. Each lobe secretes different hormones in response to signals from the hypothalamus.

Initially, both the atria and ventricles are relaxed (diastole). 
The P wave represents depolarization of the atria and is followed by atrial contraction (systole).

Relationship between the Cardiac Cycle and ECG-2 
Atrial systole extends until the QRS complex where they relax. 
The QRS complex represents ventricles depolarization and followed by ventricular contraction. 
The T wave represents ventricles repolarization and marks the beginning of ventricular relaxation.

In step one, which is labeled at rest, the plot line is steady at negative seventy millivolts. In step 2, a stimulus is applied, causing the plot line to increase to positive 30 millivolts. The curve sharply increases at step three, labeled voltage rises. After peaking at positive thirty, the plot line then quickly drops back to negative 70. This is the fourth step, labeled voltage falls. The plot line continues to drop below negative 70 and this is step 5, labeled end of action potential. Finally, the plot line gradually increases back to negative seventy millivolts, which is step 6, labeled return to rest.

Structures of Nervous System
The nervous system can be divided into two major regions: the central and peripheral nervous systems.
The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord.
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is everything else.

Basic Function of Nervous Tissue
Three components:
Sensation: receiving information about the environment to gain input about what is happening outside the body (or, sometimes, within the body). 

The sensory functions register the presence of a change from homeostasis or a particular event in the environment, known as a stimulus.

Atomic structure 
Atoms are made up of three subatomic particles:
Protons  
Positively charged (+)
Have 1 atomic mass unit (1 amu)
Neutrons  
No charge (neutral)
Have 1 amu
Electrons  
Negatively charged ()
Are so tiny they have virtually no weight (1/2000 amu)
Easy Concept

occurrences.slide_text:
Atoms structure 
Atoms are neutral since the number of protons equal the number of electrons. 
Since protons and neutrons are heavy, they are located in the center of the atom which is the nucleus.
Since electrons are lighter, they constantly spin around the nucleus
The positive proton attracts them to stay around but not within the nucleus. 
Easy Concept

Most abundant in body tissues.
Composed of three fatty acids and one glycerol molecule
Main functions
Major fuel source for the body.
Assists the absorption and transport of the nonpolar fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Protects and cushions the body’s bones and internal organs, and acts as insulation to retain body heat.

Atoms (1)
Different elements contain different numbers of subatomic particles.
Each atom has a unique number of neutron. 
Electrons spin around the nucleus in energy levels called electron shells.
Electron shells have different number of electrons.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This four panel figure shows four different atoms with the electrons in orbit around the nucleus.
occurrences.slide_text:
Atoms (2)
The far the electron from the nucleus, the more energy it has and the easiest to separate from the atom.
Atoms can have up to 7 electron shells. We will study only three. 
Each shell can hold limited number of electrons:
1st shell holds up to 2 electrons 
2nd shell holds up to 8 electrons
3rd shell holds up to 18 electrons 
Electrons fill the lower shell before moving to higher one
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This four panel figure shows four different atoms with the electrons in orbit around the nucleus.
occurrences.slide_text:
Role of Electrons (1)
The outer shell is called the valence shell.
Atoms are most stable when they have 8 electrons in their valence shell. This is known as the octet rule. 
Since electrons tend to leave the atom, they control the ability of the atom to participate in chemical reactions.
The atoms are neutral since the number of protons equal the number of electrons. Any changes in electron number will change the charge of the atom.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This four panel figure shows four different atoms with the electrons in orbit around the nucleus.
occurrences.slide_text:
Role of Electrons (2)
Most of the atoms do not have 8 electrons in their valence shell.
Because of the octet rule, atoms engage in chemical reactions to either gain, lose or share electron(s) and have 8 electrons in their valence shell.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
Ionic bonds (1)
When atoms lose or gain electrons they become Ions
In ions the number of protons and electrons is not equal
Atoms lose or gain electron to have 8 electrons in their valence shell.
If the atom loses an electron or more it becomes a cation. Cations are positively charged ions. 
If the atom gains an electron or more it becomes an anion. Anions are negatively charged ions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the orbit model of a sodium atom and a chlorine atom and arrows pointing towards the transfer of electrons from sodium to chlorine to form sodium and chlorine ions.
occurrences.slide_text:
Ionic bonds (2)
A classical example of ionic bond is the table salt or NaCl. 
Na donates its lonely electron in its valence shell to have only 8 electrons in the 2nd level (the new valence shell). Na will become a cation. 
Cl accepts the donated electron to have 8 in its valence shell and becomes an anion.  
The opposite charges of anion and cation result in attraction between the two atoms. This attraction is the Ionic Bond.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: 207_Ionic_Bonding-01.jpg
occurrences.slide_text:
Ionic bonds (3)
Salts in general are results of ionic bond. 
Salts are crystals when dry.
Salts are easily disassociate in water and ions will be released. 
The Na+ and Cl- once disassociated they remain ions (Na does not get its electron back!)
+

occurrences.alt: This figure shows three water molecules and the hydrogen bonds between them.
occurrences.slide_text:
Hydrogen bonds
Formed when a weakly positive hydrogen atom already bonded to one electronegative atom (for example, the oxygen in the water molecule) is attracted to another electronegative atom from another molecule. 
In other words, hydrogen bonds always include hydrogen that is already part of a polar molecule.
Video
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure of a water molecule. The top panel shows two oxygen atoms and one hydrogen atom with electrons in orbit and the shared electrons. The middle panel shows a three-dimensional model of a water molecule and the bottom panel shows the structural formula for water.
occurrences.slide_text:
Polar covalent bonds
H2O is a classical example of polar molecule
Oxygen has more attraction force (electronegative) for the electrons, so it pulls the shared electrons from the 2 hydrogen atoms.
 O will display partial 2 (d−) negative charges and each H will display a partial 1 (d+) positive charge.
Electrons spend more time around the oxygen atom and less time around the hydrogen atom. 
Water as a molecule has no charge.

occurrences.slide_text:
Proteins Function as Enzymes (2)
Enzymes work by lowering the activation energy required for a given chemical reaction to occur.
This increases the speed of the chemical reactions.

occurrences.alt: The figure shows a dehydration-synthesis reaction.
occurrences.slide_text:
Water in Chemical Reactions (2)
In dehydration synthesis, one reactant gives up an atom of hydrogen and another reactant gives up a hydroxyl group (OH) in the synthesis of a new product. In the formation of their covalent bond, a molecule of water is released as a byproduct .
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: the panel shows a hydrolysis reaction.
occurrences.slide_text:
Water in Chemical Reactions (3)
In hydrolysis, a molecule of water disrupts a compound, breaking its bonds. The water is itself split into H and OH. One portion of the severed compound then bonds with the hydrogen atom, and the other portion bonds with the hydroxyl group.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the chemical structure of phospholipids.
occurrences.slide_text:
Phospholipids
Phospholipid is a bond between the glycerol component of a lipid and a phosphorous molecule.
Two fatty acid chains and glycerol attached to a phosphate group. 
The nonpolar fatty acids and the polar phosphate group creates two distinct ends in the phospholipid molecule. 
Head (the phosphor group) is hydrophilic
Tails (the fatty acids) are hydrophobic
Important in cell membrane structure
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the chemical structure of cholesterol
occurrences.slide_text:
Steroids
The most important contribution to human structure and function is cholesterol 
Cholesterol is an important component of bile acids, compounds that help emulsify dietary fats.
Building block of many hormones.
Found in the cell membrane
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
pH: Acid-base concentration 
The relative acidity or alkalinity of a solution can be indicated by its pH.
pH measures the concentrations of H+. 
Acidic solutions have lower pH and high concentrations of H+.
pH range: 0-6.99
Basic solutions have higher pH and low H+ concentrations
pH range: 7.01-14
Neutral solutions have pH of 7.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows four beakers containing different liquids.
occurrences.slide_text:
Bases
A substance that accepts H+ already present in solution
Basic substances combine with H+ present to form a water molecule, thereby removing H+ and reducing the solution’s acidity.
In many cases when a base dissolved in water it releases OH–
Example: NaOH → Na+ + OH–
Important bases 
Bicarbonate ion (HCO3–) 
and ammonia (NH3)

occurrences.slide_text:
Salts (1)
Formed from ionic bonds
Dissociates completely in water
The positive and negative regions on the water molecule (the hydrogen and oxygen ends respectively) attract the negative chloride and positive sodium ions, pulling them away from each.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows a crystal lattice of sodium chloride interacting with water to form a hydrated sodium ion and a hydrated chloride ion.
occurrences.slide_text:
Salts (2)
These ions are electrolytes; they are capable of conducting an electrical current in solution.
critical to the function of ions in transmitting nerve impulses and prompting muscle contraction.
Ions plays essential role in homeostasis
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure of nucleotides.
occurrences.slide_text:
Nucleotides
Nucleotide is composed of three subunits:
one or more phosphate groups
a pentose sugar: either deoxyribose or ribose
a nitrogen-containing base: adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine, or uracil
Nucleotides can be assembled into nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) or the energy compound adenosine triphosphate.
Deoxyribose (in DNA)                Ribose (in RNA)

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure of an amino acid.
occurrences.slide_text:
Proteins (2)
An amino acid is a molecule composed of an amino group and a carboxyl group, together with a variable side chain. 
20 different amino acids contribute to nearly all of the thousands of different proteins important in human structure and function.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure of sucrose, lactose, and maltose.
occurrences.slide_text:
Disaccharides
A disaccharide is a pair of monosaccharides.
formed via dehydration synthesis.
glucose + fructose → sucrose + water
Important disaccharides
Sucrose; table sugar, maltose; malt sugar, lactose; milk sugar
Body breaks them through hydrolysis in order to digest them.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure of glucose, fructose, galactose, deoxyribose, and ribose.
occurrences.slide_text:
Monosaccharides
A monosaccharide is a monomer of carbohydrates.
Usually referred to as simple sugars.
Monomers of carbohydrates
Essential monosaccharides in human body
Hexose sugars; have 6 carbon atoms
Glucose (blood sugar), fructose, and galactose
Pentose sugars; have 5 carbon atoms
Ribose and deoxyribose
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure of starch, glycogen, and cellulose.
occurrences.slide_text:
Polysaccharides
Polysaccharides can contain a few to a thousand or more monosaccharides.
Important polysaccharides
Starch: polymers of glucose. In plant-based foods and are relatively easy to digest.
Glycogen: polymers of glucose in animals’ tissues especially in muscles and liver.
Cellulose: is the component of plant food referred to as “fiber”. In humans, cellulose/fiber is not digestible; however, dietary fiber has many health benefits

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the chain structures of a saturated and an unsaturated fatty acid.
occurrences.slide_text:
Triglycerides or Neutral Fats (2)
Saturated fatty acids: have no double carbon bonds.
These straight, rigid chains pack tightly together and are solid or semisolid at room temperature
Butter and lard are examples
Increase the risk of heart disease
Unsaturated fatty acids: have one double carbon bond.
Liquid at room temperature. 
Olive oil and Omega-3 are examples
Reduce the risk of heart disease

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a straight chain
occurrences.slide_text:
Shape of Proteins (1)
Protein’s shape is essential to its function
Proteins are not functional till they have a 3D shape that makes them specific.
As a key that opens one lock because of its groves, the 3D structure enables the protein to bind to its target. 
A protein’s shape is determined by the sequence of amino acids of which it is made.
The sequence is called the primary structure of the protein.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the secondary structure of peptides. The top panel shows a straight chain, the middle panel shows an alpha-helix and a beta sheet. The bottom panel shows the tertiary structure and fully folded protein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Shape of Proteins (2)
The secondary structure, which can take the form of an alpha-helix or a beta-pleated sheet, is maintained by hydrogen bonds between amino acids in different regions of the original polypeptide strand.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the secondary structure of peptides. The top panel shows a straight chain, the middle panel shows an alpha-helix and a beta sheet. The bottom panel shows the tertiary structure and fully folded protein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Shape of Proteins (3)
The tertiary structure occurs as a result of further folding and bonding of the secondary structure. 
Some small proteins are functional at this level.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the secondary structure of peptides. The top panel shows a straight chain, the middle panel shows an alpha-helix and a beta sheet. The bottom panel shows the tertiary structure and fully folded protein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Shape of Proteins (4)
The quaternary structure occurs as a result of interactions between two or more tertiary subunits. 
The example shown here is hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells which transports oxygen to body tissues.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
Proteins Function as Enzymes (1)
Enzymes: proteins that catalyse chemical reactions
There is a specifically matched enzyme for each substrate and, thus, for each chemical reaction
Substrate should match the 3D shape of the active site (key and lock/jigsaw puzzle)

occurrences.slide_text:
Nucleic Acids
The nucleic acids differ in their type of pentose sugar.
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is nucleotide that stores genetic information.
Ribonucleic acid (RNA) is a ribose-containing nucleotide that helps manifest the genetic code as protein.


Deoxyribose (in DNA)                                      Ribose (in RNA)

occurrences.slide_text:
ATP: Adenosine Triphosphate
Is composed of a ribose sugar, an adenine base, and three phosphate groups
ATP is classified as a high energy compound because the two covalent bonds linking its three phosphates store a significant amount of potential energy.
Structure of ATP
Adenine-containing RNA nucleotide with two additional phosphate groups

occurrences.slide_text:
ATP
When a phosphate group is cleaved from ATP, the products are adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and inorganic phosphate (Pi).
ATP usage in the body 
Muscle contraction
Transport of substances and ions in and out of cells 
Anabolic chemical reactions

occurrences.alt: This figure shows a double helix.
occurrences.slide_text:
DNA
Two strands of DNA coil around each other to form double helix structure. 
DNA is strictly located in cell nucleus 
Nitrogen base is one of four : 
Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C) or Thymine (T)
A pairs with T.
C pairs with G.

Acids
A substance that releases hydrogen ions (H+) in solution
Hydrogen ions are protons  since they have no electrons. In solution, H+ are very likely to participate in chemical reaction. 
Examples of acids
HCl (hydrochloric acid): strongest acid. H2CO3 (carbonic acid): weak acid, important in human body

A test, called a hematocrit, measures the percentage of RBCs or erythrocytes, in a blood sample.
Upon spinning blood tube, three layers will formed
Erythrocytes at the bottom of tube. 
42-52% in males
37-47% in females
Buffy coat: contains WBCs. Less than 1%

During the first pregnancy, the Rh− mother can be exposed to the baby’s Rh+ cells.
The mother’s immune system begins to generate anti-Rh antibodies

Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN) -2
If the mother conceive another Rh+ baby, the Rh antibodies she has produced can cross the placenta into the fetal bloodstream and destroy the fetal RBCs. 
It can cause fetus death in the womb or shortly after birth.

occurrences.slide_text:
Hemoglobin-1
Hemoglobin is a large molecule made up of proteins and iron. 
It consists of four folded chains of a protein called globin. 
Each of these globin molecules is bound to a red pigment molecule called heme, which contains an ion of iron (Fe2+).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
Hemoglobin-2
Each iron ion in the heme can bind to one oxygen molecule; therefore, each hemoglobin molecule can transport four oxygen molecules. 
An individual erythrocyte may contain about 300 million hemoglobin molecules, and therefore can bind to and transport up to 1.2 billion oxygen molecules

occurrences.slide_text:
Disorders of Erythrocytes-2
Easy Concept
Anemias caused by faulty or decreased RBC production include sickle cell anemia, iron deficiency anemia, vitamin deficiency anemia, and diseases of the bone marrow and stem cells.
Sickle-cell anemia	
A characteristic change in the shape of erythrocytes.
Assume a sickle (or crescent) shape, especially at low oxygen concentrations
Caused by mutated hemoglobin, so it is genetic disorder.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows micrographs of the  neutrophil
occurrences.slide_text:
Neutrophils
The most common of all the leukocytes. Comprise 50–70 percent of total leukocyte count. Significantly larger than erythrocytes. 
The nucleus has 2-5 lobes
Phagocytic cells specialized in bacterial infection.  
Abnormally high counts of neutrophils indicate infection and/or inflammation, particularly triggered by bacteria.
Low counts may be caused by drug toxicity and other disorders, and may increase an individual’s susceptibility to infection.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows micrographs of the  basophil
occurrences.slide_text:
Basophils
Less than 1% of the total leukocyte count. 
Contain many large granules that make it difficult to see the two-lobed nucleus.
Basophils intensify the inflammatory response. 
They release histamine, which contribute to inflammation and acts as vasodilator, and heparin, which opposes blood clotting.
High counts of basophils are associated with allergies, parasitic infections, and hypothyroidism. 
Low counts are associated with pregnancy, stress, and hyperthyroidism.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows micrographs of the  lymphoctyte
occurrences.slide_text:
Lymphocytes
The second most common type of leukocyte, 20–30% of all leukocytes.
Essential for the immune response. 
Three major groups: Natural Killer (NK) cells, B cells, and T cells (also called B and T lymphocytes).
NK cells recognize cells that do not express “self” proteins. 
B and T cells, T cells play prominent roles in defending the body against specific pathogens like viruses and cancer. B cells produce antibodies.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows micrographs of the monocyte
occurrences.slide_text:
Monocytes
Normally represent 2–8 percent of the total leukocyte count. 
They are significantly larger than other leukocytes with unique horseshoe-shaped nuclei. 
Macrophages are monocytes that have left the circulation and phagocytize debris, foreign pathogens, worn-out or damaged cells. 
Macrophages release antimicrobial chemicals that attract other leukocytes to the site of an infection.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This flowchart shows a myeloid stem cell differentiating into platelets.
occurrences.slide_text:
Platelets
A platelet is a fragment of the cytoplasm of a cell called a megakaryocyte.
Platelets are relatively small, 2–4 μm in diameter, but numerous, with typically 150,000–160,000 per μL of blood.
Critical to stoppage of blood flow following damage to a vessel. 
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
Blood Group Detection-1
Blood is mixed with the three antibodies: A, B and D.
In case the corresponding antigen is present, the antibodies will adhere to it causing agglutination of RBCs. 
A+ blood type

occurrences.slide_text:
Eosinophil
2–4% of total leukocyte count. 
The nucleus has 2-3 lobes with red to orange granules.
The granules contain antihistamine molecules, which counteract the activities of histamines ( inflammatory chemicals produced by basophils and mast cells). 
Phagocytic cells that fight parasitic worms. 
High counts of eosinophils are typical of patients experiencing allergies, parasitic worm infestations, and some autoimmune diseases. 
Low counts may be due to drug toxicity and stress.

The gray mantle of the human brain that make up most of the mass of the brain
The wrinkled portion is the cerebral cortex.

The postcentral gyrus, the primary somatosensory cortex.
The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex.

The temporal lobe is associated with primary auditory sensation and establishing long-term memory.
The main sensation associated with the parietal lobe is somatosensation, meaning the general sensations associated with the body.

occurrences.slide_text:
3-Cerebrum: Cerebral Hemispheres
Frontal lobe, is primarily associated with motor functions. The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex. Cells from this region are the upper motor neurons that instruct cells in the spinal cord to move skeletal muscles.
Anterior to these regions is the prefrontal lobe, which serves cognitive functions that can be the basis of personality, short-term memory, and consciousness.

4-The Spinal Cord
The gray matter is subdivided into regions that are referred to as horns. 
The posterior horn is responsible for sensory processing.
The anterior horn sends out motor signals to the skeletal muscles. 
The lateral horn (only in thoracic and upper lumbar regions) is the central component of the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system.

1-The Spinal Cord and Spinal Nerves
Information come and leave the spinal cord through specific roots.
Dorsal root brings sensory information from somatic and visceral organs. 
Ventral root carries out motor commands to somatic and visceral organs. 
On dorsal root the cell bodies of sensory neurons are clustered together in a ganglion

The Diencephalon
The diencephalon is deep beneath the cerebrum and constitutes the walls of the third ventricle.
Two major regions: thalamus and the hypothalamus
Other structures include epithalamus, which contains the pineal gland, and the subthalamus.

Thalamus
A collection of nuclei that relay information between the cerebral cortex and the periphery, spinal cord, or brain stem.
Sensory information going up for processing by the cortex and motor commands coming down from the cortex, all pass by the thalamus.

The midbrain, the pons and the medulla are collectively referred to as the brain stem. 
The midbrain coordinates sensory representations of the visual, auditory, and somatosensory perceptual spaces.

The pons is the main connection with the cerebellum. The pons and the medulla regulate several crucial functions, including the cardiovascular and respiratory systems and rates.

1-The Spinal Cord
The spinal cord maintains the tube structure and is only specialized into certain regions. 
Spinal cord regions are the cervical region, followed by the thoracic, then the lumbar, and finally the sacral region. 
As the vertebral column grows, these nerves grow with it and result in a long bundle of nerves that resembles a horse’s tail and is named the cauda equina.

2-Spinal Nerves
There are eight pairs of cervical nerves designated C1 to C8.
Twelve thoracic nerves designated T1 to T12.
Five pairs of lumbar nerves designated L1 to L5.
Five pairs of sacral nerves designated S1 to S5.
One pair of coccygeal nerves.

3-Spinal Nerves
Axons from different spinal nerves will come together into a systemic nerve. 
They form nerve plexus, whereas the other spinal nerves directly correspond to nerves at their respective levels. 
The word plexus is used to describe networks of nerve fibers with no associated cell bodies.

The lumbar plexus arises from all the lumbar spinal nerves and gives rise to nerves enervating the pelvic region and the anterior leg. 
The femoral nerve is one of the major nerves from this plexus, which gives rise to the saphenous nerve as a branch that extends through the anterior lower leg.

occurrences.slide_text:
Heart Anatomy-1
The human heart is located within the thoracic cavity, medially between the lungs in the space known as the mediastinum.
Sits within the pericardial cavity.
The superior surface of the heart is called the base which is located at the level of the third rib.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the location of the heart in the thorax.
occurrences.slide_text:
Heart Anatomy-2
The inferior tip of the heart is called the apex, lies between the fourth and fifth ribs 
The right side of the heart is deflected anteriorly, and the left side is deflected posteriorly.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the human heart with the arteries and veins labeled. It shows the direction of the blood flow.
occurrences.slide_text:
Chambers and circulation through the Heart
Consists of four chambers: each side have one upper chamber; atrium, and one lower chamber; ventricle. 
Each atrium acts as a receiving chamber and pushes blood into the respective ventricle. 
The ventricles serve as the primary pumping chambers, propelling blood to the lungs or to the rest of the body.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the human circulatory system.
occurrences.slide_text:
Circulation Circuits-1 
Two distinct but linked circuits: the pulmonary and systemic circuits. 
The pulmonary circuit transports blood to and from the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and delivers carbon dioxide for exhalation. 
The pulmonary circuit is short, and it is a low-pressure circulation. 
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the human circulatory system.
occurrences.slide_text:
Circulation Circuits-2 
The systemic circuit transports oxygenated blood to the rest of the body and returns deoxygenated blood and carbon dioxide to the heart. 
The systemic circuit is long and high pressure, high friction circulation
From there it will be sent back to the pulmonary circulation.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the human circulatory system.
occurrences.slide_text:
Blood Moving Out the Heart
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk, it bifurcates into the left and right pulmonary arteries which take the blood to lungs. This is part of the pulmonary circuit.
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the Aorta which branches and takes blood to the rest of the body. This is part of the systemic circuit.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the human circulatory system.
occurrences.slide_text:
Blood Coming Back to the Heart
The pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium, which pumps the blood into the left ventricle. This is part of the pulmonary circuit.
The superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava, return deoxygenated blood to the right atrium. This is part of the systemic circuit.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the human heart with the arteries and veins labeled. It shows the direction of the blood flow.
occurrences.slide_text:
Chambers and circulation through the Heart-1
Superior and inferior vena cava bring deoxygenated blood to the right atrium from all over the body.
Pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood from the lungs to left atrium.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the human heart with the arteries and veins labeled. It shows the direction of the blood flow.
occurrences.slide_text:
Chambers and circulation through the Heart-2
Pulmonary trunk (and pulmonary arteries) takes deoxygenated blood from right ventricle to lungs.
Aorta takes oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to all over the body.
Easy Concepts

occurrences.slide_text:
Membranes of the Heart-1
The pericardium or pericardial sac: consists of two distinct sublayers: 
The outer fibrous pericardium 
The inner serous pericardium.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows a magnified view of the structure of the heart wall.
occurrences.slide_text:
Membranes of the Heart-2
The fibrous pericardium is a dense connective tissue that protects the heart and maintains its position in the thorax. 
The serous pericardium is a  delicate two layers membrane: 
Parietal pericardium: fused to the fibrous pericardium.
Visceral pericardium, or epicardium: fused to the heart and is part of the heart wall. 
The pericardial cavity, filled with lubricating serous fluid, lies between the epicardium and the pericardium.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows a magnified view of the structure of the heart wall.
occurrences.slide_text:
Layers of the Heart Wall
Three layers: 
The outermost layer is the innermost layer of the pericardium, the epicardium, or the visceral pericardium.
The middle and thickest layer is the myocardium, made largely of cardiac muscle cells. Responsible for blood pump through the heart and into the major arteries. 
The innermost layer is the endocardium. It lines the chambers where the blood circulates and covers the heart valves. It is continuous with the endothelial lining of the blood vessels

occurrences.slide_text:
Internal Structure of the Heart
As mentioned earlier it has Four chambers
Two atria
Two ventricles
Interatrial septum: separates atria
Interventricular septum: separates ventricles
Atrioventricular septum separates the atria and ventricles

Easy Concepts

occurrences.slide_text:
Heart Valves-1
Specialized structure that ensures one-way flow of blood. 
Two types of valves
Atrioventricular valves located between atria and ventricles
Semilunar valves located between ventricles and major arteries
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the anterior view of the heart with the different heart valves labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Heart Valves-2
The valves between the atria and ventricles are as atrioventricular valves. 
Between right atrium and ventricle is the tricuspid valve
Between the left atrium and ventricle is the bicuspid valve or mitral valve.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the anterior view of the heart with the different heart valves labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Heart Valves-3
The valves at the openings that lead to the pulmonary trunk and aorta are known as semilunar valves. 
Between right ventricle and pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve
Between the left ventricle and the aorta is the aortic semilunar valve.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: the figure shows the location of the mitral valve in the open position in the heart.
occurrences.slide_text:
Heart Valves-4
The atrioventricular valves are attached to the walls of the ventricles through strong strands of connective tissue called the chordae tendineae which are connected to papillary muscles in the wall of the ventricles. 
chordae tendineae hold the flaps in closed position and prevent them from everting into the atria

occurrences.slide_text:
Heart Valves-5
Both atrioventricular valves open at the same time due to pressure on them from blood in atria. 
Then open toward inside because of chordae tendineae.

Disorders of Coronary Circulation
Atherosclerosis: the hardening of the arteries that involves the accumulation of plaque (fatty material including cholesterol, connective tissue, white blood cells, and some smooth muscle cells). 
The flow of blood will be restricted, a condition called ischemia that causes the cells to receive insufficient amounts of oxygen, called hypoxia. 
Cells might die leading to myocardial infraction (heat attack)

Each valve can be heard separately if the stethoscope at different is placed at different position.

occurrences.slide_text:
Electrocardiogram-3
It records the complete electrical activity of the heart, not a single AP.
ECG appears as a wave with five prominent points: the P wave, the QRS complex, and the T wave.
Each point indicates a certain activity at a certain place in the heart.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows a graph of millivolts over time and the heart cycles during an ECG.
occurrences.slide_text:
Electrocardiogram-4
The P wave represents the depolarization of the atria. 
The atria begin contracting approximately 25 ms after the start of the P wave.
P-R interval is the period between the start of atrial excitation to the start of ventricle excitation
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows a graph of millivolts over time and the heart cycles during an ECG.
occurrences.slide_text:
Electrocardiogram-5
The large QRS complex represents the depolarization of the ventricles and atria repolarization.
Ventricles require a stronger electrical signal because of their larger size. 
The ventricles begin to contract as the QRS reaches the peak of the R wave.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows a graph of millivolts over time and the heart cycles during an ECG.
occurrences.slide_text:
Electrocardiogram-6
The T wave represents the ventricles repolarization. 
Q-T interval is the period between ventricle depolarization and repolarization.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows a graph of millivolts over time and the heart cycles during an ECG.
occurrences.slide_text:
Electrocardiogram-7
S-T segment is the period of complete ventricular depolarization.
P-R segment is the time delay between atrial repolarization and ventricular depolarization. It reflects the delay at the AV node.
T-P segment complete depolarization of the entire heart. No electrical activity in the heart.
