occurrences.alt: This illustration resembles a flow chart. It begins with the sun shining on a silhouette of a man. One arrow leads from the sun to the man’s skin, stating that Vitamin D is manufactured in the skin after the absorption of sunlight. Another arrow points into the man’s mouth and states that Vitamin D is ingested through food and supplements, absorbed by the intestines, and carried to the liver via the bloodstream. A call out of the liver states that, in the liver, Vitamin D turns into 25 (OH) D, also known as calcidiol, the primary form of circulating Vitamin D. Another callout of the right kidney states that, in the kidneys, Vitamin D is transformed into 1 25 OH (D2). This is also known as calcitriol, a biologically active form of Vitamin D. The synthesis of Vitamin D facilitates calcium absorption from the small intestine, calcium re-absorption from the kidneys, and the rebuilding of bone tissue.
occurrences.slide_text:
Nutrition and Bone Tissue
Vitamin D is important for calcium reabsorption in the small intestine. 
In addition to vitamin D’s role in calcium absorption, it also plays a role, though not as clearly understood, in bone remodeling.

occurrences.alt: In this illustration, the two mechanisms that maintain calcium homeostasis are shown as two semicircles that are combined, one on top of each other, to make a complete circle. Homeostasis occurs along the diameter of the circle, at the border between the two semicircles. At homoeostasis, normal calcium levels are 10 milligrams per deciliter. The lower semicircle represents the mechanisms that increase calcium levels in the blood when the levels are too low. First, the parathyroid glands release PTH. PTH stimulates osteoclast activity, causing calcium ions to be released from bone. PTH also increases the reabsorption of calcium by the kidney. In addition, PTH also increases calcium absorption in the small intestines via Vitamin D synthesis. These three actions cause calcium ion levels in the blood to increase.
occurrences.slide_text:
Regulation of Calcium
Calcium and phosphate are both regulated through the actions of two hormones: parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcitonin. 
PTH is released from the parathyroid gland in response to low blood calcium. It activates osteoclasts to break down bone and release calcium-phosphate salts. 
PTH also increases the gastrointestinal absorption of calcium by activating vitamin D
PTH raises blood calcium levels by inhibiting the loss of calcium through the kidneys.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: In this illustration, the two mechanisms that maintain calcium homeostasis are shown as two semicircles that are combined, one on top of each other, to make a complete circle. Homeostasis occurs along the diameter of the circle, at the border between the two semicircles. At homoeostasis, normal calcium levels are 10 milligrams per deciliter. The upper semicircle represents the mechanism that reduces elevated calcium levels in the blood when the levels are too high. First, the thyroid gland releases calcitonin. Calcitonin activity inhibits osteoclasts and decreases the reabsorption of calcium ions in the kidney. These two actions cause calcium ion levels in the blood to drop back to homeostasis.
occurrences.slide_text:
Regulation of Calcium and Phosphate
Calcitonin is released from the thyroid gland in response to elevated blood levels of calcium. The hormone increases the
activity of osteoblasts, which remove calcium from the blood and incorporate calcium into the bony matrix.

Compact and Spongy Bone
The osteocytes are located inside spaces called lacunae (singular = lacuna), found at the borders of adjacent lamellae. 
Canaliculi connect with the canaliculi of other lacunae and eventually with the central canal. 
This allows nutrients to be transported to the osteocytes and wastes to be removed from them.

Sensory receptors 
Cells or structures that detect sensations. 
Stimuli from varying sources, and of different types, are received and changed into the electrochemical signals of the nervous system. 
Sensation is the activation of sensory receptor cells at the level of the stimulus. 
Perception is the central processing of sensory stimuli into a meaningful pattern.

occurrences.slide_text:
Gustation (Taste)
Five confirmed tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami (savory). 

Tongue Anatomy:
Covered with papillae; raised taste buds. 
Taste buds house gustatory receptor cells that respond to food chemicals. 
Taste Mechanisms:
Salty: Sodium ions (Na⁺) depolarize cells. 
Sour: Hydrogen ions (H⁺) trigger depolarization. 
Sweet & Bitter: Food molecules bind to G protein–coupled receptors. 
Umami: Triggered by L-glutamate (found in protein-rich foods). 
Easy Concept

Tympanic membrane (eardrum)
At the end of ear canal
Thin, cone-shaped membrane.
Vibrates in response to sound

Small cavity within the temporal bone.
Contains three bones called the ossicles:
Malleus: the “hammer,” attached to eardrum
Incus: the “anvil” links the other two
Stapes: the “stirrup,”  its base goes into oval window
Ossicles main function is to amplify sound (vibrations).

Middle ear is connected to the nasopharynx by the pharyngotympanic tube or Eustachian tube
Equalize pressure on the inner side of the tympanic membrane.
 Ear-pop is a result of the air pressure on both sides of tympanic membrane.

2-The Semicircular canals
Rotational movement of the head is encoded by the cristae ampullaris in the base of the semicircular canals. As one of the canals moves, the internal fluid moves in the opposite direction, causing the crista ampullaris to bend. The movement of two canals within a plane results in information about the direction in which the head is moving, and activation of all six canals can give a very precise indication of head movement in three dimensions.

Lacrimal apparatus
Lacrimal gland, located above the lateral side of the eye, produce tears. 
Tears flow over the conjunctiva, washing away foreign particles toward the lacrimal duct at the medial corner of the eye.
From there they drain into lacrimal sac which leads to nasal cavity.

2-Transmission of Sound Waves to Cochlea
Vibrations in the oval window stir the perilymph in the scala vestibule. This results in a wave that goes all the way to the helicotrema and comes back through the scala tympani.

2-The Cochlea
Scala vestibuli: behind the oval window and receives vibrations from it. Superior to the cochlear duct.
Scala tympani: Inferior to the cochlear duct and leads to the round window. 
Both contains the same type of lymph and merged at the helicotrema at the apex of the cochlea.

3-The Cochlea
Cochlear duct or scala media: between scala vestibule and tympani (but not open to them) and contains different form of lymph. 
Contains the organ of Corti, the organ of hearing.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

5-The Cochlea
Three membranes:
Vestibular membrane: the roof of the scala media. Separates it from scala vestibuli.
Basilar membrane: the floor of the scala media. Seperates it from the scala tympani.
Tectorial membrane: runs in the scala media and covers the organ of corti.

The maculae are specialized for sensing linear acceleration,
such as when gravity acts on the tilting head, or if the head starts moving in a straight line.

This will generate an electrical signal that is transmitted through the vestibulocochlear nerve to auditory centers in the brain.

The gradual changes in the shapes of the apical cells as the bladder fills with urine.
It is found only in the urinary system, specifically the ureters and urinary bladder.

 As the bladder the apical cells turn to squamous.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the silhouette of a female surrounded by four micrographs of tissue. Each micrograph has arrows pointing to the organs where that tissue is found. The upper left micrograph shows nervous tissue that is whitish with several large, purple, irregularly-shaped neurons embedded throughout. Nervous tissue is found in the brain, spinal cord and nerves. The upper right micrograph shows muscle tissue that is red with elongated cells and prominent, purple nuclei. Cardiac muscle is found in the heart. Smooth muscle is found in muscular internal organs, such as the stomach. Skeletal muscle is found in parts that are moved voluntarily, such as the arms. The lower left micrograph shows epithelial tissue. This tissue is purple with many round, purple cells with dark purple nuclei. Epithelial tissue is found in the lining of GI tract organs and other hollow organs such as the small intestine. Epithelial tissue also composes the outer layer of the skin, known as the epidermis. Finally, the lower right micrograph shows connective tissue, which is composed of very loosely packed purple cells and fibers. There are large open spaces between clumps of cells and fibers. Connective tissue is found in the leg within fat and other soft padding tissue as well as bones and tendons.

occurrences.alt: The left image shows a tight junction. The two cell membranes are bound by transmembrane protein strands. The proteins travel the inside edge of the right cell membrane and cross over to the left cell membrane, cinching the two membranes together. The cell membranes are still somewhat separated in between neighboring strands, creating intercellular spaces.
occurrences.slide_text:
Tight Junctions
Separates the cells into apical and basal compartments. When two
adjacent epithelial cells form a tight junction, there is no extracellular space between them and the movement of substances
through the extracellular space between the cells is blocked. This enables the epithelia to act as selective barriers.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The diagram shows a gap junction. The gap junctions are composed of two interlocking connexins, which are round, hollow tubes that extend through the cell membranes. Two connexins, one from the left cell membrane and the other from the right cell membrane, meet between the two cells, forming a connexon. Even at the site of the connexon, there is a small gap between the cell membranes. On the inside edge of the right cell membrane, the gap junction appears as a depression. Three connexins are embedded into the membranes like buttons on a shirt.
occurrences.slide_text:
Gap Junctions

Forms an intercellular passageway between the membranes of adjacent cells to facilitate the movement of fluid, small molecules and ions between the cytoplasm of adjacent cells.
These junctions allow electrical and metabolic coupling of adjacent cells, which coordinates function in large groups of cells.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left shows a desmosome. Here, the inside edge of both the right and left cell membranes have brown, round plaques. Each plaque has tentacle-like intermediate filaments (keratin) that extend into each cell’s cytoplasm. The two plaques are connected across the intercellular space by several interlocking transmembrane glycoproteins (cadherin). The connected glycoproteins look similar to a zipped-up zipper between the right and left cell membranes.
occurrences.slide_text:
Desmosomes
Desmosomes occur in patches on the membranes of cells. The patches are structural proteins on the inner surface of the cell’s membrane.
Provide strong and flexible connections.
These junctions influence the shape and folding of the epithelial tissue.

occurrences.alt:
This images shows the difference between squamous, cuboidal and columnar cells. 
simple squamous epithelium, the cells are flattened and single layered. In a simple cuboidal epithelium, the cells are cube shaped and single layered. In a simple columnar epithelium, the cells are rectangular and are attached to the basement membrane on one of their narrow sides, so that each cell is standing up like a column.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Classification of Epithelia
Cell shapes can be squamous (flattened and thin), cuboidal (boxy, as wide as it is tall), or columnar (rectangular, taller than it is wide).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure is a table showing the appearance of squamous, cuboidal and columnar epithelial tissues. Simple and compound forms are shown for each tissue type. In a simple squamous epithelium, the cells are flattened and single layered. In a simple cuboidal epithelium, the cells are cube shaped and single layered. In a simple columnar epithelium, the cells are rectangular and are attached to the basement membrane on one of their narrow sides, so that each cell is standing up like a column. There is only one layer of cells. In a pseudostratified columnar epithelium, the cells are column-like in appearance, but they vary in height. The taller cells bend over the tops of the shorter cells so that the top of the epithelial tissue is continuous. There is only one layer of cells. A stratified squamous epithelium contains many layers of flattened cells. Stratified cuboidal epithelium contains many layers of cube-shaped cells. Stratified columnar epithelium contains many layers of rectangular, column-shaped cells.

1-Classification of Epithelia
Epithelial tissues are classified according to the shape of the cells and number of the cell layers formed
The number of cell layers in the tissue can be one—where every cell rests on the basal lamina—which is a simple epithelium, or more than one, which is a stratified epithelium and only the basal layer of cells rests on the basal lamina.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows a diagram of a neuron and a micrograph showing two neuron cells. The body of the neuron contains a single, purple nucleus. The cell is irregularly shaped, having many projections emerging from its surface. Six sets of dendrites project from the top, right, and bottom edges of the cell. The dendrites are yellow and branch many times after leaving the cell, taking on the appearance of tiny trees. The axon projects from the left edge of the cell. The axon is a long cable like structure that branches into several finger like projections at its end. This is where the neuron makes contact with other cells. A label also notes that the area where the axon emerges from the cell body contains microfibrils and microtubules. The micrograph is considerably less magnified than the diagram. The neurons stain darkly and their nuclei are clearly visible. Their irregular cell body is also visible, along with the beginning of the axons.
occurrences.slide_text:
Nervous Tissue
Nervous tissue is characterized as being excitable and capable of sending and receiving  electrochemical signals that provide the body with information. 
Two main classes of cells make up nervous tissue: the neuron and neuroglia

occurrences.alt: a diagram of regular dense connective tissue alongside a micrograph. The tissue is composed of parallel, thread-like collagen fibers running vertically through the diagram. Between the vertical fibers, several dark, oval shaped fibroblast nuclei are visible. In the micrograph, the whitish collagen strands run horizontally. Several dark purple fibroblast nuclei are embedded in the lightly stained matrix.
occurrences.slide_text:
Dense Regular Connective Tissues
Tissues are parallel to each other, enhancing tensile strength and resistance to stretching in the direction of the fiber orientations. 
Ligaments and tendons are made of dense regular connective tissue, but in ligaments not all fibers are parallel.

occurrences.alt: The left image shows a diagram of connective tissue. As a whole, the connective tissue appears somewhat disorganized, with fibers and cells mixed together heterogeneously. There are many open spaces between the embedded elements, suggesting that the connective tissue is somewhat loosely packed. The thickest fibers are collagen fibers; the thinner fibers are elastic fibers. Both the collagen fibers and the elastic fibers crisscross randomly throughout the tissue. In addition, a net of reticular fibers appear in the upper part of the diagram. Two yellow and oval shaped adipocytes are embedded below the reticular fiber net, with a small dark nucleus squeezed into one corner of the cell. A mesenchymal cell is next to one of the adipocytes. The cell is rectangular and has four projections stemming from each corner of the cell. The projections appear to attach to the nearby collagen fibers. A fibroblast is located at the center of the diagram. The fibroblast appears similar to the mesenchymal cell, except that it is larger and has more projections. Finally, a white macrophage is in the lower right of the diagram. The macrophage is a white, oval shaped disc with a prominent nucleus. The right diagram is a micrograph of connective tissue. The tissue is mostly stained pink, however, the thick collagen fibers crisscrossing the tissue are white. Five adipocytes also appear white, except for their cell membrane and nucleus, which stained dark. A mesenchymal cell occupies the space between two adipocytes. It stains a very deep purple, but its shape is unclear in the micrograph. A fibrocyte is also visible as an oval shaped cell with a deep purple nucleus.

Areolar connective tissue
Shows little specialization. It contains all the cell types and fibers  previously described and is distributed in a random, web-like fashion. 
It fills the spaces between muscle fibers, surrounds blood and lymph vessels, and supports organs in the abdominal cavity. 
Areolar tissue underlies most epithelia and represents the connective tissue component of epithelial membranes, which are described further in a later section.

fibers

is a mesh-like, supportive framework for soft organs such as lymphatic tissue, the spleen, and the liver.
Reticular cells produce the reticular fibers that form the network onto which other cells attach.

Because of this, the irregular dense connective tissue appears less organized than the regular dense connective tissue. Elastic cartilage
Contains elastic fibers as well as collagen and proteoglycans.
This tissue gives rigid support as well as elasticity. 
The external ear contains elastic cartilage.

occurrences.slide_text:
3-Types of cartilage
Fibrocartilage
is tough because it has thick bundles of collagen fibers dispersed through its matrix. 
Menisci in the knee joint and the intervertebral discs are examples of fibrocartilage.

1-Types of cartilage
Hyaline cartilage
most common type of cartilage in the body, consists of short and dispersed collagen fibers and contains large amounts of proteoglycans.
Strong and flexible.
Found in the rib cage and covers bones where they meet to form moveable joints.

Bone or Osseous tissue
Bone is the hardest connective tissue. It provides protection to internal organs and supports the body.
Microscopic view of compact bone. UMICH Webscope (https://tinyurl.com/ybeootn4)

occurrences.slide_text:
Blood and Lymph
Blood and lymph are fluid connective tissues. Cells circulate in a liquid extracellular matrix.
Transport nutrients, salts, and wastes through the body.
Lymph drains into blood vessels, delivering molecules to the blood that could not otherwise directly enter the bloodstream.

Involuntary muscle

Contraction is responsible for involuntary movements in the internal organs. 
It forms the contractile component of the digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems as well as the airways and arteries. 
Each cell is spindle shaped with a single nucleus and no visible striations

1-Ureters
The renal pelvis narrows to become the ureter of each kidney.
Completely retroperitoneal and are approximately 30 cm long. 
The inner mucosa is lined with transitional epithelium
They pierce the bladder wall obliquely and create an one-way valve that allows urine into the bladder but prevents reflux of urine from the bladder back into the ureter.

occurrences.slide_text:
1-Internal Anatomy of the Kidney
The outer region called the renal cortex and an inner region called the medulla
The medulla has two distinct regions; the renal pyramids and renal papillae. 
The papillae are bundles of collecting ducts that transport urine made by nephrons to the calyces of the kidney for excretion.

2-Internal Anatomy of the Kidney
The renal hilum is the entry and exit site for structures servicing the kidneys: vessels, nerves, lymphatics, and ureters.
The renal arteries form directly from the descending aorta, whereas the renal veins return cleansed blood directly to the inferior vena cava.

occurrences.slide_text:
3-Internal Anatomy of the Kidney
Emerging from the hilum is the renal pelvis, which is formed from the major and minor calyxes in the kidney. 
The renal pelvis funnels urine into the ureter.

Emerging from the hilum is the renal pelvis, which is formed from the major and minor calyxes in the kidney. 
The renal pelvis funnels urine into the ureter.
Urine flow: Renal pyramid  minor calyx  major calyx renal pelvis  ureter

Gross Anatomy of the Kidney
Lie on either side of the spine in the retroperitoneal space between the parietal peritoneum and the posterior abdominal wall.
They are roughly the size of a fist and well vascularized.
On the superior aspect of each kidney is the adrenal gland. 
The adrenal cortex directly influences renal function through the production of the hormone aldosterone to stimulate sodium reabsorption

Cortical nephrons: 
85% of total nephrons. 
Located in the cortex.
Juxtamedullary nephrons: 
15 % of total nephrons. 
Located between the cortex and medulla. Their loop of Henle extends deep in the medulla. 
Produce concentrated urine. 






By Artwork by Holly Fischer - http://open.umich.edu/education/med/resources/second-look-series/materials - Urinary Tract Slide 20, 26, CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=24367127

occurrences.slide_text:
1-Nephron Parts
Renal Corpuscle
Tuft of capillaries called the glomerulus that is largely surrounded by Bowman’s (glomerular) capsule.
Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) 
Nephron loop (loop of Henle)
Distal convoluted tubule (DCT)
Distal convoluted tubule lead to collecting duct. 




By Artwork by Holly Fischer - http://open.umich.edu/education/med/resources/second-look-series/materials - Urinary Tract Slide 20, 26, CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=24367127

occurrences.slide_text:
4-Nephron Parts
Renal Corpuscle
Tuft of capillaries called the glomerulus that is largely surrounded by Bowman’s (glomerular) capsule.
The glomerulus is a high-pressure capillary bed between afferent and efferent arterioles.
Bowman’s capsule surrounds the glomerulus to form a lumen, and captures and directs this filtrate to the PCT.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top panel of this image shows the cross section of the juxtaglomerular apparatus. The major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Nephron Parts-Renal Corpuscle
The outermost part of Bowman’s capsule, the parietal layer, is a simple squamous epithelium. 
The visceral layer of the capsule is made out of unique cells named Podocytes.
Podocytes have finger like extensions (pedicels) that covers the glomerular capillaries.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this figure shows an image of a podocyte. The right panel shows a tube-like structure that illustrates the filtration slits and the cell bodies.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Nephron Parts-Renal Corpuscle
The outermost part of Bowman’s capsule, the parietal layer, is a simple squamous epithelium. 
The visceral layer of the capsule is made out of unique cells named Podocytes.
Podocytes have finger like extensions (pedicels) that covers the glomerular capillaries.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The figure shows a tube-like structure with the basement membrane and other parts labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Nephron parts-filtration membrane
The main function of the glomerulus is to filter blood. This happen through a filtration membrane. 
The filtration membrane is made out of three layers (deep to superficial):
The glomerular capillaries have fenestrations (windows) on them. Substances less than 8 nm can pass these windows
Basement membrane 
The pedicels form filtration slits, small gaps between them.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the different ions and chemicals that are secreted and reabsorbed along the nephron. Arrows show the direction of the movement of the substance.
occurrences.slide_text:
Nephron Parts-Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)
Filtered fluid collected by Bowman’s capsule enters into the PCT. 
PCT walls are made of simple cuboidal cells with microvilli to increase surface area and maximize solutes absorption and secretion of solutes (Na+, Cl–, glucose, etc.).
These cells actively transport ions across their membranes, so they possess a high concentration of mitochondria in order to produce sufficient ATP.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the different ions and chemicals that are secreted and reabsorbed along the nephron. Arrows show the direction of the movement of the substance.
occurrences.slide_text:
Nephron Parts-Loop of Henle
Thick portions of the nephron loop consists of simple cuboidal epithelium.
The thin portions simple squamous epithelium. 
The descending loop is responsible for absorbing water 
The ascending loop is responsible for absorbing Na+/K+/Cl– and secreting urea into urine. No water absorption or secretion in the ascending loop.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the different ions and chemicals that are secreted and reabsorbed along the nephron. Arrows show the direction of the movement of the substance.
occurrences.slide_text:
Nephron Parts-Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)
Shorter than the PCT.
Cells are not as active as in PCT.
Absorption occur under the influence of hormones
Aldosterone cause Na+ absorption ( Cl- follows)
PTH causes Ca++ absorption. 
Other ions like HCO3- and H2O are also absorbed.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the different ions and chemicals that are secreted and reabsorbed along the nephron. Arrows show the direction of the movement of the substance.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Collecting Ducts
Continuous with the nephron but not part of it.
Several nephrons empty in same collecting duct.
Run through medullary pyramids
Deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the different ions and chemicals that are secreted and reabsorbed along the nephron. Arrows show the direction of the movement of the substance.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Collecting Ducts
Cells lining the collecting duct have ADH receptors. 
ADH results in increasing water channel proteins (aquaporin) on these cells which lead to increase absorption of H2O.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text: Nephron physiology
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows an aquaporin water channel in the bilayer membrane with water molecules passing through.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Collecting Ducts
Cells lining the collecting duct have ADH receptors. 
ADH results in increasing water channel proteins (aquaporin) on these cells which lead to increase absorption of H2O.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the different ions and chemicals that are secreted and reabsorbed along the nephron. Arrows show the direction of the movement of the substance.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Tubular Reabsorption and Secretion 
PCT, nephron loop, DCT an collecting ducts are places for reabsorption and secretion of various solutes at different places.
Both mechanisms could be passive or active, depending on size, concentration gradient and presence of hormones.
The descending loop absorb water,  but the ascending loop absorbs electrolytes
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the different ions and chemicals that are secreted and reabsorbed along the nephron. Arrows show the direction of the movement of the substance.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Tubular Reabsorption and Secretion 
Most of the Ca++, Na+, glucose, and amino acids must be reabsorbed by the nephron to maintain homeostatic plasma concentrations. 
Other substances, such as urea, K+, ammonia (NH3), creatinine, and some drugs are secreted into the filtrate as waste products.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the different pressures acting across the glomerulus.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Glomerular Filtration
At glomerulus, there are several hydrostatic pressures (pressure produced by a fluid against a surface)
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure: blood pressure within the glomerular capillaries. 
Blood colloid osmotic pressure: Osmotic pressure in Bowman’s capsule (blood has higher solute concertation comparing to the filtrate in Bowman’s capsule )
Capsular hydrostatic pressure: pressure created by fluid within the capsule (due to space limit)
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the different pressures acting across the glomerulus.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Glomerular Filtration
Glomerular filtration occurs when glomerular (blood) hydrostatic pressure exceeds the capsular  hydrostatic pressure and the blood colloid osmotic pressure. 
The (net) of all of the pressures, results in a net filtration pressure (NFP).
On Image it would be 55-(30+15)=10
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the different pressures acting across the glomerulus.

occurrences.slide_text:
Arteries
An artery is a blood vessel that conducts blood away from the heart. 
They have relatively thick walls that can withstand the high pressure of blood ejected from the heart. 
Elastic arteries are the close to heart arteries. They have the thickest walls and contain a high percentage of elastic fibers. 
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top panel shows the cross-section of a large vein, the middle panel shows the cross-section of a medium sized vein, and the bottom panel shows the cross-section of a venule.
occurrences.slide_text:
Veins
A vein is a blood vessel that conducts blood toward the heart. 
They are thin-walled vessels with large and irregular lumens. 
Because they are low-pressure vessels, larger veins are commonly equipped with valves to ensure unidirectional flow of blood toward the heart and prevent backflow.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows a capillary bed connecting an arteriole and a venule.
occurrences.slide_text:
Capillary Beds
A capillary is a microscopic channel that supplies blood to the tissues. 
Their walls are leaky to allow substances to pass through. 
The precapillary sphincters, circular smooth muscle cells that surround the capillary tightly regulate the flow of blood to the capillaries.
Easy Concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a micrograph with the cross sections of an artery and a vein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Structure of Blood Vessel Wall-1
Each type of vessel has a lumen—a hollow passageway through which blood flows.
Arteries have smaller lumens than veins. This helps to maintain blood pressure. 
Their thicker walls and smaller diameters give arterial lumens a more rounded appearance in cross section than the lumens of veins.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this figure shows the ultrastructure of an artery, and the right panel shows the ultrastructure of a vein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Structure of Blood Vessel Wall-2
Both arteries and veins have the same three distinct tissue layers, called tunics.
From the most interior layer to the outer, these tunics are 
The tunica intima.
The tunica media.
The tunica externa
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this figure shows the ultrastructure of an artery, and the right panel shows the ultrastructure of a vein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Tunica Intima
The tunica intima (also called the tunica interna) is composed of epithelial and connective tissue layers. 
Its lined with specialized simple squamous epithelium called the endothelium.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this figure shows the ultrastructure of an artery, and the right panel shows the ultrastructure of a vein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Tunica Media-1
Generally the thickest layer in arteries, and it is much thicker in arteries than it is in veins. 
Consists of layers of smooth muscle supported by connective tissue that is primarily made up of elastic fibers, most of which are arranged in circular sheets.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this figure shows the ultrastructure of an artery, and the right panel shows the ultrastructure of a vein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Tunica Media-2
Contraction and relaxation of the circular muscles decrease and increase the diameter of the vessel lumen.
When contract (vasoconstriction), they increase blood pressure as the lumen narrows
When relax (vasodilation), they decrease blood pressure as the lumen widen
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this figure shows the ultrastructure of an artery, and the right panel shows the ultrastructure of a vein.
occurrences.slide_text:
Tunica Externa
Also called the tunica adventitia, is a substantial sheath of connective tissue composed of collagenous fibers with some elastic fibers.
In veins it contains groups of smooth muscle. 
This is the thickest tunic in veins and may be thicker than the tunica media in some larger arteries.

occurrences.slide_text:
Components of Arterial Blood Pressure
Easy Concepts
Arterial blood pressure in the larger vessels consists of several distinct components: systolic and diastolic pressures, pulse pressure, and mean arterial pressure.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This graph shows the value of pulse pressure in different types of blood vessels.
occurrences.slide_text:
Systolic and Diastolic Pressures-1
Easy Concepts
Blood pressure is expressed as systolic pressure over diastolic pressure. 
The systolic pressure is the higher value (typically around 120 mm Hg) and reflects the arterial pressure resulting from the ejection of blood during ventricular contraction, or systole. 
The diastolic pressure is the lower value (usually about 80 mm Hg) and represents the arterial pressure of blood during ventricular relaxation, or diastole.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This graph shows the value of pulse pressure in different types of blood vessels.
occurrences.slide_text:
Systolic and Diastolic Pressures-2
Easy Concepts
Pulse Pressure: the difference between the systolic pressure and the diastolic pressure. It represents the force that the heart generates each time it contracts.
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) represents the “average” pressure of blood in the arteries. Important in determining the amount of blood delivered to a capillary bed in a tissue.

Blood Pressure in Venous System-2
Skeletal Muscle Pump
The pressure within the veins can be increased by the contraction of the surrounding skeletal muscle.
This helps the lower-pressure veins counteract the force of gravity, increasing pressure to move blood back to the heart.
Veins valves prevent the blood backflow.

occurrences.slide_text:
Lymphatic capillaries
Easy concepts
Vessels where interstitial fluid enters the lymphatic system to become lymph fluid. 
Located in almost every tissue in the body.
Interlaced among the arterioles and venules of the circulatory system.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
Larger Lymphatic Vessels, Trunks, and Ducts
The lymphatic capillaries empty into larger lymphatic vessels.
eventually merge to form larger lymphatic vessels known as lymphatic trunks
Easy concepts

occurrences.slide_text:
1-Structure of the Lymphatic System
Easy concepts
The lymphatic vessels are open-ended capillaries, which feed into larger and larger lymphatic vessels.
They empty into the bloodstream by a series of ducts.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows a female human body, and the entire lymphatic system is shown. The right panel shows magnified images of the thymus and the lymph node. All the major parts in the lymphatic system are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Structure of the Lymphatic System
Easy concepts
Along the way, the lymph travels through the lymph nodes, which are commonly found near the groin, armpits, neck, chest, and abdomen. 
Humans have about 500–600 lymph nodes throughout the body
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the structure of a lymph node.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Lymphoid Node
Lymph nodes function to remove debris and pathogens from the lymph “filters of the lymph”.
The lymph node is also the site of adaptive immune responses mediated by T cells, B cells, and accessory cells of the adaptive immune system.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the structure of a lymph node.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Lymphoid Node
Surrounded by a tough capsule of connective tissue.
Separated into compartments by trabeculae, the extensions of the capsule. 
The structural support of the lymph node is provided by a series of reticular fibers laid down by fibroblasts.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the structure of a lymph node.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Lymphoid Node
The major routes into the lymph node are via afferent lymphatic vessels. 
Cells and lymph fluid that leave the lymph node may do so by another set of vessels known as the efferent lymphatic vessels.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the structure of a lymph node.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Lymphoid Node
Flow speed is reduced by:
Mesh of reticular fibers 
The difference in numbers of afferent and efferent lymphatic vessels 
Reducing flow speed is important to allow the immune cells to examine the lymph for any antigens or pathogens.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the structure of a lymph node.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-Lymphoid Node
Within the cortex there are lymphoid follicles, which contains rapidly dividing B cells surrounded by a layer of T cells .
As the lymph continues to flow through the node, it enters the medulla, which consists of  B cells and plasma cells.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

Easy concepts
The B cell undergoes nearly all of its development in the red bone marrow
Bone Marrow Red bone marrow fills the head of the femur, and a spot of yellow bone marrow is visible in the center.

Prominent in kids and small in adult.

1-Spleen
A major secondary lymphoid organ.
A fragile organ without a strong capsule and is dark red due to its extensive vascularization.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows a close up view of the location of the spleen. The right panel shows the blood vessels and spleen tissue.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Spleen
Divided by trabeculae. 
Within each splenic nodule is:
an area of red pulp consisting of mostly red blood cells  
Its primarily functions as a filtration system of the blood, using cells of the relatively nonspecific immune response.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
3-Spleen
Divided by trabeculae. 
Within each splenic nodule is:
An area of white pulp, which resembles the lymphoid follicles of the lymph nodes.
It is the place for where adaptive T and B cell responses are mounted.

Tonsils
Located along the inner surface of the pharynx and are important in developing immunity to oral pathogens
The pharyngeal tonsil swells upon infection due to an active immune response.
Other tonsils include the Palatine and Lingual tonsils
