occurrences.slide_text:
Respiration 
Can be divided into four processes:
Pulmonary ventilation: The movement of air in and out of the lungs.
External respiration: exchange of O2 and CO2 between lungs and blood
Transport of O2 and CO2 in blood
Internal respiration: exchange of O2 and CO2 between blood and cells
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this image shows a person inhaling air and the location of the chest muscles. The right panel shows the person exhaling air and the contraction of the thoracic cavity.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Pulmonary Ventilation
Pulmonary ventilation comprises two major steps: inspiration and expiration. 
Inspiration is the process that causes air to enter the lungs, and expiration is the process that causes air to leave the lungs
Respiratory cycle is one sequence of inspiration and expiration.
Two muscle groups are used during normal inspiration: the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the upper half of the human body. The major organs in the respiratory system are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Respiratory System
Functionally, the respiratory system can be divided into:
The conducting zone: includes the organs and structures not directly involved in gas exchange. 
The respiratory zone: where gas exchange occurs 
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the upper half of the human body. The major organs in the respiratory system are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Organs of Respiratory System
Based on location, respiratory system is divided into: 
Upper respiratory: include nose and adjacent structures and pharynx
Lower respiratory: include: larynx, trachea, bronchi and branches, lungs and alveoli.

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the human nose. The top left panel shows the front view, and the top right panel shows the side view. The bottom panel shows the cartilaginous components of the nose.
occurrences.slide_text:
Nose
The major entrance and exit for the respiratory system.
Two major sections: the external nose, and the nasal cavity or internal nose.
It moistens and filters the air coming into the body.
Holds receptors for smelling.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top panel of this figure shows the trachea and its organs. The major parts including the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Trachea
The trachea (windpipe) extends from the larynx toward the lungs.
Formed by 16 to 20 stacked, C-shaped pieces of hyaline cartilage that are connected by dense connective tissue.
The trachea branches into the right and left primary bronchi.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top panel of this figure shows the trachea and its organs. The major parts including the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Trachea
The primary bronchi enter the lungs at the hilum, a concave region where blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves also enter the lungs.
A bronchial tree (or respiratory tree) is the multiple-branched bronchi. 
The main function of the bronchi, like other conducting zone structures, is to provide a passageway for air to move into and out of each lung.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the side view of the face. The different parts of the pharynx are color-coded and labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Pharynx
The pharynx is a tube formed by skeletal muscle and lined by mucous membrane that is continuous with that of the nasal cavities.
Divided into three major regions: the nasopharynx, the oropharynx, and the laryngopharynx
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The this figure shows the anterior view of the larynx,
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Larynx
Easy Concept
The larynx is a cartilaginous structure inferior to the laryngopharynx that connects the pharynx to the trachea.
Regulates the volume of air that enters and leaves lungs.
Three large cartilage pieces form the major structure of the larynx: the thyroid cartilage (anterior), epiglottis (superior), and cricoid cartilage (inferior).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: the panel shows the right lateral view of the larynx.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Larynx
The thyroid cartilage makes up the wall of larynx.
The thick cricoid cartilage forms a ring connects larynx to trachea.
The epiglottis is made of elastic cartilage and covers the opening of the trachea to prevent entry of solid objects.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the larynx. The different types of cartilages are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Larynx
Easy Concept
When epiglottis closes, its unattached end rests on the glottis. 
The glottis is composed of the vestibular folds, the true vocal cords, and the space between these folds.
By I, Welleschik, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2468726
1=vocal folds, 2=vestibular fold, 3=epiglottis, 4=plica aryepiglottica, 5=arytenoid cartilage, 6=sinus piriformis, 7=dorsum of the tongue
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the bronchioles and alveolar sacs in the lungs and depicts the exchange of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the pulmonary blood vessels.
occurrences.slide_text:
Bronchiole
Bronchi keeps branching and declines in diameter to form bronchioles (1 mm diameter).
Bronchioles do not contain cartilage in their wall as bronchi. 
Wall contains smooth muscles to increase or decrease airflow 
The terminal bronchioles leads to the site of gas exchange.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the bronchioles and alveolar sacs in the lungs and depicts the exchange of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the pulmonary blood vessels.
occurrences.slide_text:
Respiratory Zone
Includes structures that are directly involved in gas exchange.
Begins where the terminal bronchioles join a respiratory bronchiole, the smallest type of bronchiole.
Respiratory bronchiole leads to an alveolar duct, opening into a cluster of alveoli.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the bronchioles and alveolar sacs in the lungs and depicts the exchange of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the pulmonary blood vessels.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Alveoli
An alveolar duct is a tube composed of smooth muscle and connective tissue, which opens into an alveolar sac. 
An alveolar sac is a cluster of many individual alveoli that are responsible for gas exchange.
An alveolus is one of the many small, grape-like sacs that are attached to the alveolar ducts.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the detailed structure of the alveolus. The top panel shows the alveolar sacs and the bronchioles. The middle panel shows a magnified view of the alveolus.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Alveoli
Has elastic walls that allow the alveolus to stretch during air intake, which greatly increases the surface area available for gas exchange. 
Alveoli are connected to their neighbors by alveolar pores, which help maintain equal air pressure throughout the alveoli and lung.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the detailed structure of the alveolus. The top panel shows the alveolar sacs and the bronchioles. The middle panel shows a magnified view of the alveolus.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Alveoli
The alveolar wall consists of three major cell types:
Type I alveolar cells: squamous epithelial cells and are highly permeable to gases. 
Type II alveolar cells: interspersed among the type I cells and secretes pulmonary surfactant, a substance composed of phospholipids and proteins that reduces the surface tension of the alveoli. 
Alveolar macrophage roams around the alveolar and removes debris and pathogens that have reached the alveoli.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: Cross section of an alveoli and capillaries showing diffusion of gases.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-Alveoli
Easy Concept
Type I alveolar cells is attached to a thin, elastic basement membrane which is extremely thin and borders the endothelial membrane of capillaries. 
The alveoli and capillary membranes form a respiratory membrane that is approximately 0.5 mm thick. 
By Delmalani18 - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=69613938
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure of the lungs with the major parts labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-The Lungs
The right lung consists of three lobes: the superior, middle, and inferior lobes. 
The left lung consists of two lobes: the superior and inferior lobes.
Oblique fissure separates the superior and inferior lobes of the left lung and the middle and inferior lobes of the right lung.
Horizontal fissure separates the superior and middle lobes of the right lung. 
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the lungs and the chest wall, which protects the lungs, in the left panel. In the right panel, a magnified image shows the pleural cavity and a pleural sac.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Lungs
The main function of the lungs is to perform the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide with air from the atmosphere.
Pyramid-shaped, paired organs that are connected to the trachea.
Rest on the diaphragm.
The right lung is shorter and wider than the left lung, and the left lung occupies a smaller volume than the right. 
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the lungs and the chest wall, which protects the lungs, in the left panel. In the right panel, a magnified image shows the pleural cavity and a pleural sac.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Lungs
The cardiac notch is an indentation on the surface of the left lung, and it allows space for the heart. 
The apex of the lung is the superior region, whereas the base is the opposite region near the diaphragm. 
Each lung is composed of smaller units called lobes. Fissures separate these lobes from each other.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: In the panel, a magnified image shows the pleural cavity and a pleural sac.
occurrences.slide_text:
Pleura of the Lungs
The pleura (plural = pleurae) is a  two layers serous membrane that surrounds the lung. 
The visceral pleura is superficial to the lungs, and extends into and lines the lung fissures.
The parietal pleura is the outer layer that connects to the thoracic wall, the mediastinum, and the diaphragm. 
The pleural cavity is the space between the visceral and parietal layers.

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this image shows a person inhaling air and the location of the chest muscles. The right panel shows the person exhaling air and the contraction of the thoracic cavity.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Pulmonary Ventilation
The expansion of the thoracic cavity forces the lungs to stretch and expand. 
Increase in volume leads to a decrease in intra-alveolar pressure, creating a pressure lower than atmospheric pressure. 
As a result, a pressure gradient is created that drives air into the lungs.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this image shows a person inhaling air and the location of the chest muscles. The right panel shows the person exhaling air and the contraction of the thoracic cavity.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Pulmonary Ventilation
In expiration, the thoracic cavity forces the lungs to shrink. 
Decrease in volume leads to a increase in intra-alveolar pressure, creating a pressure higher than atmospheric pressure. 
As a result, a pressure gradient is created that drives air out of the lungs.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this image shows a person inhaling air and the location of the chest muscles. The right panel shows the person exhaling air and the contraction of the thoracic cavity.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Pulmonary Ventilation
Air flows into the lungs largely due to a difference in pressure; atmospheric pressure is greater than intra-alveolar pressure, and intra-alveolar pressure is greater than intrapleural pressure.
Air flows out of the lungs during expiration based on the same principle; pressure within the lungs becomes greater than the atmospheric pressure.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the lungs and the air pressure in different regions.
occurrences.slide_text:
The Process of Breathing
Pulmonary ventilation is the act of breathing, which can be described as the movement of air into and out of the lungs.
The major mechanisms that drive pulmonary ventilation are atmospheric pressure (Patm); the air pressure within the alveoli, called intra-alveolar pressure (Palv); and the pressure within the pleural cavity, called intrapleural pressure (Pip).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the lungs and the air pressure in different regions.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Pressure Relationships
Gases move from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure. 
The reference point for ventilation is the atmospheric pressure which equals 760mmHg.
Because the alveoli are connected to the atmosphere via the tubing of the airways, the intrapulmonary pressure of the alveoli always equalizes with the atmospheric pressure (difference is 0).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the lungs and the air pressure in different regions.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Pressure Relationships
Intrapleural pressure is the pressure of the air within the pleural cavity.
Due to certain characteristics of the lungs, the intrapleural pressure is always lower than the intra-alveolar pressure and atmospheric pressure). 
It remains approximately –4 mm Hg throughout the breathing cycle.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows two canisters containing a gas. The two canisters show how volume and pressure are inversely proportional, which illustrates Boyle’s law.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Pressure Relationships
In a gas, pressure is a force created by the movement of gas molecules that are confined.
Boyle’s law describes the inverse relationship between volume and pressure in a gas at a constant temperature. 
If volume increases, pressure decreases. 
if volume decreases, pressure increases.
Pulmonary ventilation is dependent on three types of pressure Patm, Palv & Pip
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows a graph of different respiratory volumes. The right panel shows how the different respiratory volumes result in respiratory capacity.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Respiratory Volumes and Capacities
Respiratory volume is the term used for various volumes of air moved by or associated with the lungs at a given point in the respiratory cycle.
Four major types:
Tidal volume (TV) is the amount of air that normally enters the lungs during quiet breathing, which is about 500 milliliters.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows a graph of different respiratory volumes. The right panel shows how the different respiratory volumes result in respiratory capacity.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Respiratory Volumes and Capacities
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is the amount of air that can forcefully exhale past a normal tidal expiration, up to 1200 milliliters for men. 
Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) is produced by a deep inhalation, past a tidal inspiration. This is the extra volume that can be brought into the lungs during a forced inspiration.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows a graph of different respiratory volumes. The right panel shows how the different respiratory volumes result in respiratory capacity.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Respiratory Volumes and Capacities
Residual volume (RV) is the air remains in the lungs all the time. RV keeps lungs open.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows a graph of different respiratory volumes. The right panel shows how the different respiratory volumes result in respiratory capacity.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Respiratory Volumes and Capacities
Additional respiratory volumes :
Total lung capacity (TLC) is the sum of all of the lung volumes (TV, ERV, IRV, and RV), which represents the total amount of air a person can hold in the lungs after a forceful inhalation. TLC is about 6000 mL air for men, and about 4200 mL for women. 
Vital capacity (VC) is the amount of air a person can move into or out of his or her lungs, and is the sum of all of the volumes except residual volume (TV, ERV, and IRV), which is between 4000 and 5000 milliliters.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel shows a graph of different respiratory volumes. The right panel shows how the different respiratory volumes result in respiratory capacity.
occurrences.slide_text:
Respiratory Volumes and Capacities
Additional respiratory volumes :
Inspiratory capacity (IC) is the maximum amount of air that can be inhaled past a normal tidal expiration, is the sum of the tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume. 
Functional residual capacity (FRC): is the amount of air that remains in the lung after a normal tidal expiration; it is the sum of expiratory reserve volume and residual volume.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The left panel of this figure shows a canister of oxygen. The middle panel shows a canister of nitrogen. The right panel shows a canister containing a mixture of oxygen and nitrogen. A pressure gauge on each container shows the pressure exerted by the gas in that container.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Gas Exchange
Partial pressure (Px) is the pressure of a single type of gas in a mixture of gases. 
For example, in the atmosphere, oxygen exerts a partial pressure, and nitrogen exerts another partial pressure, independent of the partial pressure of oxygen.
Total pressure is the sum of all the partial pressures of a gaseous mixture.
Gas will move from an area where its partial pressure is higher to an area where its partial pressure is lower. 
The greater the partial pressure difference between the two areas, the more rapid is the movement of gases.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
2-Gas Exchange
External respiration:  is the exchange of gases with the external environment and occurs in the alveoli of the lungs. 
Performed by respiratory system
Internal respiration: is the exchange of gases with the internal environment and occurs in the tissues. 
Performed by cardiovascular system
The actual exchange of gases occurs due to simple diffusion.
By Ahmed Katsha. Made with Biorender
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the pathway in which external respiration takes place. The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveolus and blood plasma is detailed.
occurrences.slide_text:
External Respiration
Majority of the oxygen is picked up by erythrocytes (red blood cells) and binds to hemoglobin
Small amount is able to dissolve directly into plasma.
External respiration occurs due to partial pressure differences in oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and the blood in the pulmonary capillaries.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows how carbon dioxide is transported from the tissue to the red blood cell.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-CO2 Transportation
CO2 transportation involves the production of bicarbonate HCO3-, which is an important molecule in controlling blood pH.
Most bicarbonate is produced in erythrocytes. 
Carbonic anhydrase (CA) causes carbon dioxide and water to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into two ions: bicarbonate (HCO3–) and hydrogen (H+). The following formula depicts this reaction:
CO2 + H2O ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3 −
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows how carbon dioxide is transported from the tissue to the red blood cell.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-CO2 Transportation
About 20 percent of carbon dioxide is bound by hemoglobin and is transported to the lungs. 
Carbon dioxide does not bind to iron as oxygen does; instead, it binds to the globin portions of hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin.
The following formula depicts this reversible reaction:
CO2 + Hb ↔ HbCO2
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram details the pathway of internal respiration. The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between a red blood cell and a tissue cell is shown.
occurrences.slide_text:
Internal Respiration
Carbon dioxide is transported by three major mechanisms. 
The first mechanism is by blood plasma, as some carbon dioxide molecules dissolve in the blood. 7-10% of total CO2
The second mechanism is transport in the form of bicarbonate (HCO3–), which also dissolves in plasma. 70% of total CO2
The third mechanism is by binding to hemoglobin. 20% of total CO2
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top panel of this figure shows normal lung tissue, and the bottom panel shows lung tissue inflamed by asthma.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Disease of Respiratory System: Asthma
Asthma is a chronic disease characterized by inflammation and edema of the airway, and bronchospasms which can inhibit air from entering the lungs.
In addition, excessive mucus secretion can occur, which further contributes to airway occlusion. 
Cells of the immune system, such as eosinophils, may also be involved in infiltrating the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles.

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top panel of this figure shows normal lung tissue, and the bottom panel shows lung tissue inflamed by asthma.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Disease of Respiratory System: Asthma
Bronchospasms occur periodically and lead to an “asthma attack.” 
May be triggered by  environmental factors such as dust, pollen, pet hair, or dander, changes in the weather, mold, tobacco smoke, and respiratory infections, or by exercise and stress.
Symptoms of an asthma attack involve coughing, shortness of breath, wheezing, and tightness of the chest. Severe attacks require immediate medical attention.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: Normal Lungs and Lungs With COPD
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Diseases of the Respiratory System
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): is a type of obstructive lung disease characterized by long-term breathing problems and poor airflow.
An ongoing cough or a cough that produces a lot of mucus; this is often called smoker's cough.
Shortness of breath, especially with physical activity
Wheezing or a whistling or squeaky sound when you breathe
Chest tightness

https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health-topics/copd
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: Microscope image shows Emphysema
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Diseases of the Respiratory System
COPD includes two main conditions: emphysema and chronic bronchitis. 
Emphysema: involves damage to the air sacs (alveoli) in the lungs so the body doesn’t get enough O2.
By Nephron - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=7935360
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: Normal Lungs and Lungs With Bronchitis
occurrences.slide_text:
5-Diseases of the Respiratory System
Chronic bronchitis is an ongoing cough that lasts for several months and comes back two or more years in a row.
The lining of the airways stays constantly inflamed. This causes the lining to swell and produce more mucus, which can make it hard to breathe. 
By National Heart Lung and Blood Institute - National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=29583164
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the digestive system of a human being, with the major organs labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Function of Digestive System
Main functions of the digestive system
Break down the foods 
Release their nutrients
Absorb those nutrients
Remove the indigestible materials
It functions cooperatively with the other systems of the body.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the digestive system of a human being, with the major organs labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Digestive System Organs
Digestive system can be divided into two groups of organs:
Alimentary canal organs 
Accessory digestive organs. 
Accessory digestive are critical for orchestrating the breakdown of food and the assimilation of its nutrients into the body. 
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the digestive system of a human being, with the major organs labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Alimentary Canal Organs
Also called the gastrointestinal (GI) tract or gut.
is a one-way tube begins at the mouth and terminates at the anus.
The main function of the organs of the alimentary canal is to nourish the body. 
The canal is modified as the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, and small and large intestines to fit the functional needs of the body.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the digestive system of a human being, with the major organs labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Accessory Structures
The organs that not forming the canal.
Aid in breakdown of the food. 
Teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the digestive system of a human being, with the major organs labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Organs of Digestive System
Alimentary canal organs include esophagus, stomach, small and large intestine and rectum with anal canal.
Accessory digestive organs include mouth and teeth, liver and gallbladder, and pancreas

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the different processes involved in digestion. The image shows how food travels from the mouth through the major organs. Associated textboxes list the different processes such as propulsion, chemical and mechanical digestion and absorption near the organs where they take place.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Digestive System Processes and Regulation
Digestive system uses mechanical and chemical activities to break food.
Processes include
Ingestion
Propulsion
Peristalsis
Mechanical digestion
Chemical digestion 
Absorption
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the different processes involved in digestion. The image shows how food travels from the mouth through the major organs. Associated textboxes list the different processes such as propulsion, chemical and mechanical digestion and absorption near the organs where they take place.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Digestive System Processes and Regulation
Ingestion: the entry of food into the alimentary canal through the mouth. 
The food is chewed and mixed with saliva enzymes that breakdown the carbohydrates.
Propulsion: the movement of food through the digestive tract. 
It includes both the voluntary process of swallowing and the involuntary process of peristalsis.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the different processes involved in digestion. The image shows how food travels from the mouth through the major organs. Associated textboxes list the different processes such as propulsion, chemical and mechanical digestion and absorption near the organs where they take place.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Digestive System Processes and Regulation
Mechanical digestion: breaks the food to smaller pieces.
Includes mastication in mouth.
In stomach it creates an acidic “soup” called chyme.  
Segmentation: contractions of circular muscles. 
Contractions isolate sections of the intestine, moving their contents back and forth.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the different processes involved in digestion. The image shows how food travels from the mouth through the major organs. Associated textboxes list the different processes such as propulsion, chemical and mechanical digestion and absorption near the organs where they take place.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-Digestive System Processes and Regulation
Absorption: takes place primarily within the small intestine. 
Most nutrients are absorbed from the lumen of the alimentary canal into the bloodstream 
Defecation: undigested materials are removed from the body as feces.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the peristaltic movement of food. In the left image, the food bolus is towards the top of the esophagus and arrows pointing downward show the direction of movement of the peristaltic wave. In the center image, the food bolus and the wave movement are closer to the center of the esophagus and in the right image, the bolus and the wave are close to the bottom end of the esophagus.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Digestive System Processes and Regulation
Peristalsis: consists of sequential, alternating waves of contraction and relaxation of alimentary wall smooth muscles, which act to propel food along. These waves also play a role in mixing food with digestive juices.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram identifies the functions of mechanical and chemical digestion and absorption at each organ. Next to each organ, a callout identifies which steps of digestion take place in that particular organ.
occurrences.slide_text:
Chemical Digestion
Large food molecules (for example, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and starches) must be broken down into subunits that are small enough to be absorbed by the lining of the alimentary canal. 
This is accomplished by enzymes through hydrolysis.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows a cross-section of the stomach, and the major parts: the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Stomach
Four main regions in stomach: the cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus.
The cardia is the point where the esophagus connects to the stomach. 
Fundus is the dome-shaped region that is inferior to the diaphragm, above and to the left of the cardia. Below the fundus is the body, the main part of the stomach. 

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows a cross-section of the stomach, and the major parts: the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Stomach

The pylorus connects the stomach to the duodenum. 
The pyloric sphincter controls stomach emptying. 
In absence of food, the stomach deflates inward, and its mucosa and submucosa fall into a large fold called a ruga.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows a cross-section of the stomach, and the major parts: the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Stomach Wall
Stomach wall has an additional muscular layer called the oblique muscle.
This will cause the muscle to vigorously churn food, mechanically breaking it down into smaller particles.
The mixture of food and gastric juice that leave the stomach is called Chyme.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the cross section of the alimentary canal. The different layers of the alimentary canal are shown as concentric cylinders with major muscles and veins labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Histology of the Alimentary Canal
Alimentary tract is composed of the same four tissue layers (deep to surface):
Mucosa
Submucosa 
Muscularis
Serosa
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the cross section of the alimentary canal. The different layers of the alimentary canal are shown as concentric cylinders with major muscles and veins labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Histology of the Alimentary Canal
Mucosa: referred to as a mucous membrane.
The membrane consists of epithelium, which is in direct contact with ingested food, and the lamina propria, a layer of connective tissue analogous to the dermis.
Secretes mucus, digestive enzymes, and hormones
Absorbs final products of digestion
Protects against foodborne bacteria
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the cross section of the alimentary canal. The different layers of the alimentary canal are shown as concentric cylinders with major muscles and veins labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Histology of the Alimentary Canal
Submucosa connects the mucosa to the muscularis. 
A dense connective tissue layer that contains blood and lymphatic vessels and submucosal glands that release digestive secretions.
Serves as a conduit for a dense network of nerves known as the submucosal plexus which regulate digestive secretions and reacting to the presence of food.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the cross section of the alimentary canal. The different layers of the alimentary canal are shown as concentric cylinders with major muscles and veins labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Histology of the Alimentary Canal
Muscalaris: made up of a double layer of smooth muscle: an inner circular layer and an outer longitudinal layer.
 The contractions of these layers promote mechanical digestion, expose more of the food to digestive chemicals, and move the food along the canal.
The stomach has a third layer called oblique muscle.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the cross section of the alimentary canal. The different layers of the alimentary canal are shown as concentric cylinders with major muscles and veins labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-Histology of the Alimentary Canal
Serosa superficial to the muscularis. 
Present only in abdominal cavity.
It consists of a layer of visceral peritoneum overlying a layer of loose connective tissue.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the abdomen. The peritoneum is made distinguishable from the abdominal organs through darker lines.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Peritoneum
A serous membranous sac that hold digestive organs within the abdominal cavity.
Composed of parietal peritoneum, which lines the abdominal wall, and the visceral peritoneum, which envelopes the abdominal organs.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the abdomen. The peritoneum is made distinguishable from the abdominal organs through darker lines.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Peritoneum
The first portion of the small intestine (called the duodenum), the pancreas, and portions of the large intestine described as retroperitoneal. 
They are completely or partially posterior to the peritoneum.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the structure of the mouth. The teeth, lips, tongue, gums and many other parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Organs of Digestive System
The cheeks, tongue, and palate frame the mouth, which is also called the oral cavity
It is the place where the first process of mechanical and chemical digestion takes place.
Associated organs include the tongue, salivary glands and teeth
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the structure of the mouth. The teeth, lips, tongue, gums and many other parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Organs of Digestive System
The tongue is a strong muscle in the mouth. 
During the course of your lifetime, you have two sets of teeth (one set of teeth is a dentition). 
Your 20 deciduous teeth, or baby teeth, first begin to appear at about 6 months of age. 
Between approximately age 6 and 12, these teeth are replaced by 32 permanent teeth.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the location of the salivary glands with reference to the teeth. The different salivary glands are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Organs of Digestive System
Three major salivary glands produce saliva.
95.5% of saliva is water. 
The rest is a complex mixture of ions, glycoproteins, enzymes, growth factors, and waste products.
Salivary amylase: initiates the breakdown of carbohydrates.	
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross-section of a human face and highlights the location of the pharynx, which runs from the nostrils to the esophagus and the larynx.
occurrences.slide_text:
Pharynx
Pharynx (throat) is involved in both digestion and respiration.
When food enters the pharynx, involuntary muscle contractions close off the air passageways.

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross-section of a human face and highlights the location of the pharynx, which runs from the nostrils to the esophagus and the larynx.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Esophagus
A muscular tube that connects the pharynx to the stomach.
Posterior to the trachea, and remains in a collapsed form when not engaged in swallowing.
Penetrates the diaphragm through an opening called the esophageal hiatus.

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross-section of a human face and highlights the location of the pharynx, which runs from the nostrils to the esophagus and the larynx.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Esophagus
Food passes from the esophagus into the stomach at the lower esophageal sphincter (also called the gastroesophageal or cardiac sphincter).
The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes to let food pass into the stomach, and then contracts to prevent stomach acids from backing up into the esophagus.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the pancreas and its major parts. A magnified view of a small region of the pancreas shows the pancreatic islet cells, the acinar cells and the pancreatic duct.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Pancreas
A curious mix of exocrine (secreting digestive enzymes) and endocrine (releasing hormones into the blood) functions.
Connect the alimentary canal with the duodenum.
Secrets a mix of enzymes known as pancreatic juice.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the pancreas and its major parts. A magnified view of a small region of the pancreas shows the pancreatic islet cells, the acinar cells and the pancreatic duct.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Pancreas
The exocrine part of the pancreas arises as little grape-like cell clusters, each called an acinus.
Secrete enzyme-rich pancreatic juice into tiny merging ducts.
Ducts will end either in the common bile duct or in the pancreatic duct which directly open to duodenum.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the pancreas and its major parts. A magnified view of a small region of the pancreas shows the pancreatic islet cells, the acinar cells and the pancreatic duct.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-The Pancreas
Pancreatic juice contains some salts, sodium bicarbonate, and several digestive enzymes.
Sodium bicarbonate gives alkalinity to pancreatic juice (pH 7.1 to 8.2), which serves to buffer the acidic gastric juice in chyme and create an optimal environment for the activity of pH-sensitive digestive enzymes in the small intestine.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the pancreas and its major parts. A magnified view of a small region of the pancreas shows the pancreatic islet cells, the acinar cells and the pancreatic duct.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-The Pancreas
The pancreas produces protein-digesting enzymes in their inactive forms. These enzymes are activated in the duodenum.
The intestinal enzyme enteropeptidase turns trypsinogen to trypsin which in turn changes the procarboxypeptidase and chymotrypsinogen into their active forms, carboxypeptidase and chymotrypsin.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the histological cross-section of the stomach. The left panel shows the stomach and the center panel shows a magnified view of a small region including the epithelium and the gastric glands. The right panel shows a further magnification of the mucosa and the different cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Stomach Wall
The superficial mucosa layer consists only of surface mucus cells, which secrete a protective coat of alkaline mucus. 
Mucosa is filled with gastric pits which mark  the entry to each gastric gland, which secretes a complex digestive fluid referred to as gastric juice.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a further magnification of the mucosa and the different cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Gastric Glands Cells
The superficial mucosa layer consists only of surface mucus cells, which secrete a protective coat of alkaline mucus. 
Mucosa is filled with gastric pits which mark  the entry to each gastric gland, which secretes a complex digestive fluid referred to as gastric juice.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a further magnification of the mucosa and the different cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Gastric Glands Cells
The walls of the gastric pits are made up primarily of mucus cells secrete mucus and several hormones, including most of the stimulatory hormone gastrin.
Other cells include parietal cells, chief cells, and enteroendocrine cells.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a further magnification of the mucosa and the different cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Gastric Glands Cells
Parietal cells produce both hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor (IF). 
HCl is responsible for the high acidity (pH 1.5 to 3.5) of the stomach juice and is needed to activate the protein-digesting enzyme, pepsin. 
The acidity also kills bacteria ingested with food and helps to denature proteins, making them more available for enzymatic digestion.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a further magnification of the mucosa and the different cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Gastric Glands Cells
Intrinsic factor is a glycoprotein necessary for the absorption of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
B12 is involved in:
The maturation of red blood cells.
DNA synthesis.
Plays a role in myelin synthesis 
Producing IF is the only one stomach function necessary to life.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a further magnification of the mucosa and the different cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-Gastric Glands Cells
Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the inactive or proenzyme form of pepsin. 
Enteroendocrine cells found in the gastric glands secrete various hormones including gastrin which activates the production of HCl.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagrams shows the human digestive system and identifies the role of each organ in protein digestion. A text call-out next to each organ details the specific function.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Protein Digestion
Starts in the stomach, where HCl and pepsin break proteins into smaller polypeptides. 
In small intestine, pancreatic enzymes including chymotrypsin and trypsin, act on specific bonds in amino acid sequences.
The brush border secrete enzymes which further break down peptide chains.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the small intestine. The different parts of the small intestine are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Small Intestine
Small intestine is the place where most digestion and absorption occurs. 
About 3.05 meters (10 feet) long in a living person.
The folds and projections in the lining of the small intestine work to give it an enormous surface area.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the small intestine. The different parts of the small intestine are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Small Intestine
Subdivided into three regions. From proximal (at the stomach) to distal, these are the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.
Duodenum:  beneath the pyloric sphincter, is the area where the chyme mixed with bile and pancreatic enzymes.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the small intestine. The different parts of the small intestine are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-The Small Intestine
Jejunum and ileum have similar structure and function. 
The ileum joins the cecum, the first portion of the large intestine, at the ileocecal sphincter (or valve)
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: Illustration (a) shows the histological cross-section of the small intestine. The left panel shows a small region of the small intestine, along with the blood vessels and the muscle layers. The middle panel shows a magnified view of a small region of the small intestine, highlighting the absorptive cells, the lacteal and the goblet cells. The right panel shows a further magnified view of the epithelial cells including the microvilli. Illustrations (b) shows a micrograph of the circular folds, and illustration (c) shows a micrograph of the villi. Illustration (d) shows an electron micrograph of the microvilli.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Small Intestine Histology
The wall of the small intestine is composed of the same four layers typically present in the alimentary system. 
 Three features of the mucosa and submucosa make small intestine unique.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: Illustration shows the histological cross-section of the small intestine.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Small Intestine Histology
Circular folds are deep ridges in the mucosa and submucosa. Their shape causes the chyme to spiral, rather than move in a straight line, through the small intestine. Spiraling slows the movement of chyme and provides the time needed for nutrients to be fully absorbed.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text:
2-Small Intestine Histology
Circular folds are deep ridges in the mucosa and submucosa. Their shape causes the chyme to spiral, rather than move in a straight line, through the small intestine. Spiraling slows the movement of chyme and provides the time needed for nutrients to be fully absorbed.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The middle panel shows a magnified view of a small region of the small intestine, highlighting the absorptive cells, the lacteal and the goblet cells.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Small Intestine Histology
Villi: small (0.5-1 mm) long projections.
They increase the surface area of the epithelium tremendously. 
Each villus contains a capillary bed composed of one arteriole and one venule, as well as a lymphatic capillary.
Sugars and amino acids can enter the bloodstream directly, but lipid breakdown products are absorbed and transported to the bloodstream via the lymphatic capillary.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a further magnified view of the epithelial cells including the microvilli.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Small Intestine Histology
Microvilli are much smaller (1 µm) extensions of the plasma membrane of the mucosa’s epithelial cells.
Their combined microscopic appearance is termed as brush border. 
On their surface enzymes that finish digesting carbohydrates and proteins. 
There are an estimated 200 million microvilli per square millimeter of small intestine, greatly expanding the surface area of the plasma membrane and thus greatly enhancing absorption.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows an electron micrograph of the microvilli.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-Small Intestine Histology
Microvilli are much smaller (1 µm) extensions of the plasma membrane of the mucosa’s epithelial cells.
Their combined microscopic appearance is termed as brush border. 
On their surface enzymes that finish digesting carbohydrates and proteins. 
There are an estimated 200 million microvilli per square millimeter of small intestine, greatly expanding the surface area of the plasma membrane and thus greatly enhancing absorption.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The middle panel shows a magnified view of a small region of the small intestine, highlighting the absorptive cells, the lacteal and the goblet cells.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Intestinal Glands
The mucosa between the villi is dotted with deep crevices that each lead into a tubular intestinal crypt.
Within the crypt, several cells produce different types of secretion. 
Goblet cells produce mucus. 
Enteroendocrine cells secrete digestive hormones.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The middle panel shows a magnified view of a small region of the small intestine, highlighting the absorptive cells, the lacteal and the goblet cells.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Intestinal Glands
The submucosa of the duodenum has duodenal glands which produce a bicarbonate-rich alkaline mucus that buffers the acidic chyme as it enters from the stomach.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the histological cross section of the large intestine. The left panel shows a small region of the large intestine. The center panel shows a magnified view of this region, highlighting the openings of the intestinal glands. The right panel shows a further magnified view, with the microvilli and goblet cells.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Large Intestine Histology
Wall of the large intestine has more intestinal glands comparing to small intestine.
Two main cells
Goblet cells: secrete mucus that eases the movement of feces and protects the intestine from the effects of the acids and gases produced by enteric bacteria. 
The enterocytes absorb water and salts as well as vitamins produced by your intestinal bacteria.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the large intestine; the major parts of the large intestine are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Large Intestine
The large intestine is the terminal part of the alimentary canal. 
The primary function of this organ is to finish absorption of nutrients and water, synthesize certain vitamins, form feces, and eliminate feces from the body.
Runs from appendix to anus
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the large intestine; the major parts of the large intestine are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Large Intestine
Subdivisions: 
Cecum: a sac-like structure that is suspended inferior to the ileocecal valve. 
Receives chyme from small intestine. 
Appendix is attached to it and serves as a reservoir for intestinal bacteria.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the large intestine; the major parts of the large intestine are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-The Large Intestine
Colon: Three parts: ascending, transverse and descending. Descending colon becomes sigmoid colon before reaching the rectum.
Rectum: contains rectal valves that help separate the feces from gas to prevent the simultaneous passage of feces and gas.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the large intestine; the major parts of the large intestine are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-The Large Intestine
Anal canal: includes two sphincters. 
The internal anal sphincter is made of smooth muscle, and its contractions are involuntary. 
The external anal sphincter is made of skeletal muscle, which is under voluntary control. 
Except when defecating, both usually remain closed.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the Taenia Coli, haustra and epiploic appendages, which are parts of the large intestine.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Large Intestine Anatomy
Three unique features:
Teniae coli: three bands of smooth muscle that make up the longitudinal muscle layer of the muscularis of the large intestine.
Tonic contractions of the teniae coli bunch up the colon into a succession of pouches called haustra (singular = haustrum), which are responsible for the wrinkled appearance of the colon.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the Taenia Coli, haustra and epiploic appendages, which are parts of the large intestine.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Large Intestine Anatomy
Epiploic appendages: are small, fat-filled sacs of visceral peritoneum attached to the teniae coli called.
The purpose of these is unknown.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the accessory organs of the digestive system. The liver, spleen, pancreas, gallbladder and their major parts are shown.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Accessory Organs in Digestion
Chemical digestion in the small intestine relies on the activities of three accessory digestive organs: the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the microscopic anatomy of the liver. The top panel shows the liver; the center panel shows a magnified view of the connective tissue and the lobules. The bottom panel shows a further magnified view of a lobule, identifying the veins, bile duct and the sinusoids.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Liver
The liver is the largest gland in the body.
Divided into two primary lobes: a large right lobe and a much smaller left lobe.
The porta hepatis (“gate to the liver”) is where the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein enter the liver.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the microscopic anatomy of the liver. The top panel shows the liver; the center panel shows a magnified view of the connective tissue and the lobules. The bottom panel shows a further magnified view of a lobule, identifying the veins, bile duct and the sinusoids.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Liver
The hepatic portal vein delivers partially deoxygenated blood containing nutrients absorbed from the small intestine.
Drugs and toxins are also absorbed and processed by liver. 
Toxins- free nutrients are released into the blood, which drains into the central vein and then through the hepatic vein to the inferior vena cava.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This image shows the microscopic anatomy of the liver. The top panel shows the liver; the center panel shows a magnified view of the connective tissue and the lobules. The bottom panel shows a further magnified view of a lobule, identifying the veins, bile duct and the sinusoids.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Liver Histology
The liver has three main components: hepatocytes, bile canaliculi, and hepatic sinusoids. 
A hepatocyte is the liver’s main cell type which play a role in a wide variety of secretory, metabolic, and endocrine functions. 
Plates of hepatocytes called hepatic laminae radiate outward from the portal vein in each hepatic lobule.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a further magnified view of a lobule, identifying the veins, bile duct and the sinusoids.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Liver Histology
Bile canaliculus (plural = canaliculi) are located between adjacent hepatocytes.
These small ducts accumulate the bile produced by hepatocytes. 
Bile flows first into bile ductules and then into bile ducts.

The hepatic sinusoids combine and send blood to a central vein. Blood then flows through a hepatic vein into the inferior vena cava.

6-Liver Histology
The hepatic sinusoids contain star-shaped reticuloendothelial cells (Kupffer cells). 
These are phagocytes that remove dead red and white blood cells, bacteria, and other foreign material that enter the sinusoids. 
The portal triad is a distinctive arrangement around the perimeter of hepatic lobules, consisting of three basic structures: a bile duct, a hepatic artery branch, and a hepatic portal vein branch.

3-Liver Histology
The bile ducts unite to form the larger right and left hepatic ducts, which themselves merge and exit the liver as the common hepatic duct. 
This duct then joins with the cystic duct from the gallbladder, forming the common bile duct through which bile flows into the small intestine.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the gallbladder and its major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Gallbladder
The gallbladder stores, concentrates, and, when stimulated, propels the bile into the duodenum via the common bile duct.
When contract, the gallbladder’s contents are ejected through the cystic duct and into the bile duct.
Bile is a mixture secreted by the liver to accomplish the emulsification of lipids in the small intestine.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the gallbladder and its major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Gallbladder
Bile salts act as emulsifying agents and important for the absorption of digested lipids. 
Bile salts are reclaimed by the enterohepatic circulation. 
Once bile salts reach the ileum, they are absorbed and returned to the liver in the hepatic portal blood.

occurrences.alt: This flow chart shows the steps in digestion of carbohydrates. The different levels shown are starch and glycogen, disaccharides and monosaccharides. Under each type of sugar, examples and the enzymes responsible for digestion are listed.
occurrences.slide_text:
Carbohydrate Digestion
Starts in the mouth. 
In the small intestine, pancreatic amylase does most of starch and carbohydrate digestion.
Brush border enzymes hydrolyze disaccharides into monosaccharides.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows how lipids are absorbed from the lumen of the intestine into the lacteals. The fatty acid micelles are shown to enter the epithelial cell and form chylomicrons inside the Golgi apparatus. Then, the chylomicrons are extruded from the epithelial cell and are taken up by the lacteals.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Lipid Digestion
Starts in the mouth by lingual lipase but remain limited in its effect. Some digestion occurs also in stomach by gastric lipase.
Because the pancreas is the only consequential source of lipase, virtually all lipid digestion occurs in the small intestine.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows how lipids are absorbed from the lumen of the intestine into the lacteals. The fatty acid micelles are shown to enter the epithelial cell and form chylomicrons inside the Golgi apparatus. Then, the chylomicrons are extruded from the epithelial cell and are taken up by the lacteals.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Lipid Digestion
Pancreatic lipase breaks down each triglyceride into two free fatty acids and a monoglyceride
Lipids are emulsified within the bile and absorbed by intestine but transported through lymphatic system.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the process of segmentation in the intestines. The left panel shows the separation of chime, the middle panel shows the remixing of the chime by pushing it back together and the right panel indicates that the chime is being digested and absorbed.
occurrences.slide_text:
Mechanical Digestion in the Small Intestine
The movement of intestinal smooth muscles includes both  segmentation and a form of peristalsis called migrating motility complexes.
Segmentation separates chyme and then pushes it back together, mixing it and providing time for digestion and absorption.
