occurrences.alt: This pie chart shows that about 55% of water in the human body is intracellular fluid. About 30% of the water in the human body is interstitial fluid. Most of the remaining 15% of water is plasma, along with a small percentage labeled “other fluid”.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Fluid Compartments
Two main fluid compartments in body
Intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment includes all fluid enclosed in cells by their plasma membranes.
Extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment surrounds all cells in the body
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows a small blood vessel surrounded by several body cells. The fluid between the body cells is the interstitial fluid (IF), which is a type of extracellular fluid (ECF). The fluid in the blood vessel is also an example of extracellular fluid. The fluid in the cytoplasm of each body cell is intracellular fluid, or ICF.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Fluid Compartments
Two main ECF compartments :
Plasma: 3 L
Interstitial fluid (IF): surrounds cells not in blood
Includes: cerebrospinal fluid, lymph, synovial fluid, pleural fluid, the pericardial fluid, the peritoneal fluid, and the aqueous humor of the eye.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This bar graph shows the concentration of several ions and proteins in intracellular fluid, interstitial fluid and plasma. The ions and proteins are categories on the X axis . The Y axis shows concentration, in milliequivalents per liter, ranging from zero to 160. Three different colored bars are shown above each compound on the X axis. One bar represents intracellular fluid (ICF), a second bar represents interstitial fluid (IF, which is part of ECF) and the third bar represents plasma (ECF). Intracellular fluid contains high concentrations of K plus and HPO four two minus. It has lower concentrations of MG two plus and protein, and negligible amounts of the other compounds. Interstitial fluid contains high concentrations of NA plus and CL minus, along with a smaller amount of HCO 3 minus, and negligible amounts of the other compounds. Plasma contains large concentrations of NA plus and CL minus, with smaller concentrations of HCO 3 minus and protein, and negligible amounts of the other compounds.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Composition of Body Fluids
The compositions of the two components of the ECF are similar.
Both have high concentrations of sodium, chloride, bicarbonate. Plasma has more protein. 
ICF has elevated amounts of potassium, phosphate, magnesium, and protein. 
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This bar graph shows the concentration of several ions and proteins in intracellular fluid, interstitial fluid and plasma. The ions and proteins are categories on the X axis . The Y axis shows concentration, in milliequivalents per liter, ranging from zero to 160. Three different colored bars are shown above each compound on the X axis. One bar represents intracellular fluid (ICF), a second bar represents interstitial fluid (IF, which is part of ECF) and the third bar represents plasma (ECF). Intracellular fluid contains high concentrations of K plus and HPO four two minus. It has lower concentrations of MG two plus and protein, and negligible amounts of the other compounds. Interstitial fluid contains high concentrations of NA plus and CL minus, along with a smaller amount of HCO 3 minus, and negligible amounts of the other compounds. Plasma contains large concentrations of NA plus and CL minus, with smaller concentrations of HCO 3 minus and protein, and negligible amounts of the other compounds.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Composition of Body Fluids
Overall, the ICF contains high concentrations of potassium and phosphate ( HPO4 2 − ), whereas ECF contain high concentrations of sodium and chloride.
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This flow chart shows how potassium and sodium ion concentrations in the blood are regulated by aldosterone. Rising K plus and falling NA plus levels in the blood trigger aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone targets the kidneys, causing a decrease in K plus release from the kidneys, which reduces the amount of K plus in the blood back to homeostatic levels. Aldosterone also increases sodium reabsorption by the kidneys, which increases the amount of NA plus in the blood back to homeostatic levels.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Regulation of Sodium and Potassium
Aldosterone
Increases the excretion of potassium and the reabsorption of sodium in the kidney. 
Aldosterone is released either if:
blood levels of potassium increase
blood levels of sodium severely decrease 
blood pressure decreases.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This flow chart shows how potassium and sodium ion concentrations in the blood are regulated by aldosterone. Rising K plus and falling NA plus levels in the blood trigger aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone targets the kidneys, causing a decrease in K plus release from the kidneys, which reduces the amount of K plus in the blood back to homeostatic levels. Aldosterone also increases sodium reabsorption by the kidneys, which increases the amount of NA plus in the blood back to homeostatic levels.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Regulation of Sodium and Potassium
In the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts, aldosterone stimulates the synthesis and activation of the sodium-potassium pump 
Aldosterone net effect is to conserve and increase water levels in the plasma by reducing the excretion of sodium, and thus water, from the kidneys.
Increased osmolality of the ECF inhibits the release of the hormone (negative feedback)
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure is a top-to bottom flowchart describing the thirst response. The topmost box of the chart states that there is insufficient water in the body, which has two effects. The left branch of the chart leads to decreased blood volume, which leads to decreased blood pressure. This triggers an increase in angiotensin two. Angiotensin two stimulates the thirst center in the hypothalamus. On the right branch, insufficient water in the body leads to increased blood osmolality, which causes dry mouth. Increased blood osmolality and dry mouth is sensed by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus. This stimulates the thirst center in the hypothalamus to increase thirst, giving a person the urge to drink. Drinking decreases blood osmolality back to homeostatic levels.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Regulation of Water Intake
If the osmolality increases, the hypothalamus induce thirst. 
Hypothalamus also releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH)  which signals the kidneys to recover water from urine. 
Additionally, the hypothalamus sends signals to the salivary glands to decrease water in saliva. These changes in secretions result in a “dry mouth” and the sensation of thirst.

Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram depicts a cross section of the right wall of a kidney collecting tubule. The wall is composed of three block-shaped cells arranged vertically one on top of each other. The lumen of the collecting tubule is to the left of the three cells. Yellow-colored urine is flowing through the lumen. There is a small strip of blue interstitial fluid to the right of the three cells. To the right of the interstitial fluid is a cross section of a blood vessel. Arrows show that water in the urine is entering the left side of the wall cells through aquaporins. The water travels through the cells and then leaves the kidney tubule through additional aquaporins in the right side of the wall cells. The water travels through the interstitial space and enters into the blood in the blood vessel. The aquaporins in the wall cells are being released from aquaporin storage vesicles within their cytoplasm.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Regulation of Water Output
ADH causes the epithelial cells in the collecting tubules to display aquaporins on the cell membrane.
A diuretic is a compound that increases urine output and therefore decreases water conservation by the body.
Alcohol acts as a diuretic by inhibiting the release of ADH. Additionally, caffeine, when consumed in high concentrations, acts as a diuretic.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This photo shows the dorsal surfaces of a person’s right and left hands. The left hand is normal, with the several blood vessels visible under the skin. However, the top of the right hand is swollen and no blood vessels are visible.
occurrences.slide_text:
Disorders of Water Balance
 Edema: the accumulation of excess water in the tissues caused by water leakage from blood vessels.
Edema is almost always caused by an underlying medical condition, by the use of certain therapeutic drugs, by pregnancy, by localized injury, or by an allergic reaction.
Symptoms include swelling of the subcutaneous tissues, an increase in the normal size of the limb, and stretched, tight skin.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This illustration shows a silhouette of a human body with various organs highlighted. The percent of water contained in each organ is given. The brain typically contains 80% to 85% water, teeth contain 8% to 10% water, a single lung contains 75% to 80% water, the heart contains 75% to 80% water, the bones contain 20% to 25% water, the liver contains 70% to 75% water, the kidneys contain 80% to 85% water, the skin contains 70% to 75% water and the muscles also contain 70% to 75% water.
occurrences.slide_text:
Body Fluid Compartments
Body Water Content
In infants water forms 75% of body mass.
In adult males: water forms 60%
In adult females water forms 50%
 Water content declines to ~45% in old age
Easy Concept
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the hormone cascade that that increases kidney reabsorption of NA plus and water. In the first step, the kidneys release renin into the blood stream. The blood stream is depicted with a red arrow pointing from left to right. At the same time, the liver releases angiotensinogen into the blood, which combines with the renin, yielding angiotensin one. The blood flow then leads to the lungs. Within the pulmonary blood, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) converts angiotensin one to angiotensin two. The blood then flows to the adrenal cortex, where angiotensin two stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone. Aldosterone causes the kidney tubules to increase reabsorption of NA plus and water into the blood.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Regulation of Sodium and Potassium
Angiotensin II
Released in case of low blood pressure. 
Causes vasoconstriction and an increase in systemic blood pressure.  
Angiotensin II also signals an increase in the release of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram depicts a cross section of the left wall of a kidney proximal tubule. The wall is composed of two block-shaped cells arranged vertically one on top of each other. The lumen of the proximal tubule is to the left of the two cells. Yellow-colored urine is flowing through the lumen. There is a small strip of blue interstitial fluid to the right of the two cells. To the right of the interstitial fluid is a cross section of a blood vessel. A loop of chemical reactions is occurring in the diagram. Within the lumen of the proximal tubule, HCO three minus is combining with an H plus ion that enters the lumen from a proximal tubule cell. This reaction forms H two CO three. H two CO three then breaks into H two O and CO two, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. The CO two then moves from the lumen of the proximal tubule into one of the proximal tubule cells. There, the reaction runs in reverse, with CO two combining with H two O to form H two CO three. The H two CO three then splits into H plus and HCO three minus. The H plus moves into the lumen, reinitiating the first step of the loop. The HCO three minus leaves the proximal tubule cell and enters the blood stream.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Renal Regulation of Acid-Base Balance
The renal regulation of the body’s acid-base balance addresses the metabolic component of the buffering system.
The renal system controls the blood levels of bicarbonate.
Bicarbonate ions, HCO3 -, found in the filtrate, are essential to the bicarbonate buffer system, yet the cells of the tubule are not permeable to bicarbonate ions.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram depicts a cross section of the left wall of a kidney proximal tubule. The wall is composed of two block-shaped cells arranged vertically one on top of each other. The lumen of the proximal tubule is to the left of the two cells. Yellow-colored urine is flowing through the lumen. There is a small strip of blue interstitial fluid to the right of the two cells. To the right of the interstitial fluid is a cross section of a blood vessel. A loop of chemical reactions is occurring in the diagram. Within the lumen of the proximal tubule, HCO three minus is combining with an H plus ion that enters the lumen from a proximal tubule cell. This reaction forms H two CO three. H two CO three then breaks into H two O and CO two, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. The CO two then moves from the lumen of the proximal tubule into one of the proximal tubule cells. There, the reaction runs in reverse, with CO two combining with H two O to form H two CO three. The H two CO three then splits into H plus and HCO three minus. The H plus moves into the lumen, reinitiating the first step of the loop. The HCO three minus leaves the proximal tubule cell and enters the blood stream.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Renal Regulation of Acid-Base Balance
In order to absorb bicarbonate ion, HCO3 -, the cells must release H+ to filtrate.
There it will form carbonic acid which will enzymatically break into water and CO2
Cells capture the CO2 and convert it to bicarbonate ion which sent to blood

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the structure and the different organs in the female reproductive system. The top panel shows the lateral view and the bottom panel shows the anterior view.
occurrences.slide_text: 2-Female Reproductive Anatomy
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.slide_text: 2-Female Reproductive Anatomy
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view and the bottom panel shows the anterior view.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Ovaries
The ovaries are the female gonads.
Two regions:
Outer portion (the cortex) is composed of a tissue framework called the ovarian stroma that forms the bulk of the adult ovary.
The inner ovarian medulla is the site of blood vessels, lymph vessels, and the nerves of the ovary.
Easy concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the uterus and ovaries in the center. To the left is a micrograph showing the ultrastructure of the ovaries and to the right is a micrograph showing the ultrastructure of the uterus.
occurrences.slide_text:
The Uterine Tubes
Also called fallopian tubes or oviducts.
Serve as the conduit of the oocyte from the ovary to the uterus.
Four sections:
The isthmus: narrow medial end that is connected to the uterus. 
Ampulla: fertilization site.
The infundibulum: medial part
Fimbriae; slender and finger-like projections. Receive oocyte from ovary
Easy concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the uterus and ovaries in the center. The right is a micrograph showing the ultrastructure of the uterus.
occurrences.slide_text:
The Uterus
A muscular organ that nourishes and supports the growing embryo.
Three sections.
Fundus the superior portion of the uterus. 
The body is the middle section 
The cervix is the narrow inferior portion of the uterus that projects into the vagina. Produces mucus secretions that can facilitate sperm movement through the reproductive tract.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the uterus and ovaries in the center. The right is a micrograph showing the ultrastructure of the uterus.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Uterus Wall
Three layers. 
The serous membrane, or perimetrium: covers the exterior portion of the uterus.
Myometrium: A thick layer of smooth muscle responsible for uterine contractions.  
The endometrium innermost layer contains a connective tissue lining.
Consists of two layers: the stratum basalis and the stratum functionalis (the basal and functional layers).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This flowchart shows the formation of oocytes in the female. The top half of the flowchart is before birth and the bottom half is after puberty. A callout to the left also shows the eggs before and after sperm penetration.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Follicular phase: Oogenesis
Gametogenesis in females is called oogenesis.
Begins with the ovarian stem cells, or oogonia.
Oogonia form primary oocytes in the fetal ovary prior to birth.
The primary oocytes stop developing until the puberty
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This flowchart shows the formation of oocytes in the female. The top half of the flowchart is before birth and the bottom half is after puberty. A callout to the left also shows the eggs before and after sperm penetration.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Follicular phase: Oogenesis
After puberty, each month several of the primary oocytes undergo a second division, giving a secondary oocyte. 
Ultimately, one or two at maximum will turn into an ovum that is ready for fertilization.
 Ovulation is the release of an oocyte from the ovary
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the testis.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Testes
The male reproductive organ.
Produce both sperm and androgens, such as testosterone, and are active throughout the reproductive lifespan of the male.
Surrounded by tough dense connective tissue called tunica which forms septa that separates lobules.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the testis.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Testes
Within the lobules, sperm develop in structures called seminiferous tubules form the bulk of each testis.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the testis.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-The Testes
Seminiferous tubules contain several cell types
Spermatogenic (sperms forming) cells. These are the main cells. 
Sertoli cells. Supporting cells that secret molecules to promote sperm production
Interstitial cells located between the seminiferous tubules. 
Produce testosterone which is important in sperm maturation
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the testis.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-The Testes
Developed sperms move to straight tubules and from there into a fine meshwork of tubules called the rete testes.
Sperms then move to efferent ductules then to epididymis.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the testis.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-The Testes
Epididymis has head, body and tail.
Sperms enter at the head and move toward the tail.
Through this movement, sperms mature. 
At the tail, sperms are stored until ejaculation
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the scrotum and testes. The left panel shows the external view of the scrotum, the middle panel shows the muscle layer and the right panel shows the deep tissues of the scrotum.
occurrences.slide_text:
Scrotum
A skin-covered muscular sack called the that extends from the body behind the penis and contains testes 
This location is important in sperm production in the testes  which are kept 2 to 4°C below body temperature.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a micrograph with the cross section of a seminiferous tubule.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Spermatogenesis
The process of forming sperms
Begins at puberty, after which time sperm are produced constantly throughout a man’s life.
One production cycle, from spermatogonia through formed sperm, takes approximately 64 days. 
A new cycle starts approximately every 16 days
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows a micrograph with the cross section of a seminiferous tubule.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Spermatogenesis
Mitosis of a spermatogonial stem cell involves a single cell division that results in two identical, diploid daughter cells (spermatogonia to primary spermatocyte). 
Meiosis has two rounds of cell division: primary spermatocyte to secondary spermatocyte, and then secondary spermatocyte to spermatid. 
This produces four haploid daughter cells (spermatids).
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This diagram shows the structure of sperm; the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Structure of Formed Sperm
Sperm have a distinctive head, mid-piece, and tail region.
The head contains the extremely compact haploid nucleus with very little cytoplasm.
The midpiece is filled with mitochondria. ATP produced by these mitochondria will power the flagellum
The flagellum enables the movement of the entire sperm cell.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the steps in the regulation of testosterone production. The top panel shows the hypothalamus and the bottom panel shows two micrographs. The left micrograph is that of sertoli cells and the right micrograph is that of Leydig cells.
occurrences.slide_text: 2-Control of Testosterone
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the male reproductive system and the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Male Reproductive System
The structures of the male reproductive system include the testes, the epididymis, the penis, and the ducts and glands that produce and carry semen.
Easy concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the male reproductive system and the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Male Reproductive System
Testes (within scrotum) produce sperm
Sperm delivered to exterior through systemof ducts 
Epididymis  ductus deferens  ejaculatory duct  urethra
Easy concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the male reproductive system and the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Sperm Transport-Duct System
During ejaculation, sperm exit the tail of the epididymis and are pushed to the ductus deferens (also called the vas deferens). 
At the end of ductus deferens, the sperms enter the ejaculatory duct where they mix with semen.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the male reproductive system and the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Seminal Vesicles
Glands that contribute approximately 60 percent of the semen volume. 
Seminal vesicle fluid contains large amounts of fructose, which is used by the sperm mitochondria to generate ATP.
Semen is transported to the ejaculatory duct.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the male reproductive system and the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Prostate Gland
Anterior to the rectum at the base of the bladder surrounding the prostatic urethra.
It excretes an alkaline, milky fluid to semen that is critical to decoagulate the semen following ejaculation.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the male reproductive system and the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
Bulbourethral Glands
Two glands release a thick, salty fluid that lubricates the end of the urethra and the vagina, and helps to clean urine residues from the penile urethra. 
Their fluid is released after the male becomes sexually aroused, and shortly before the release of the semen. 
It is therefore sometimes called pre-ejaculate.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the male reproductive system and the major parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Penis
The penis is the male organ of copulation (sexual intercourse).
It is flaccid for non-sexual actions, such as urination.
The shaft of the penis surrounds the urethra.
The shaft is composed of three column-like chambers of erectile tissue that span the length of the shaft.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The image shows the uterine cycle phases.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Uterine (Menstrual) Cycle  
The Menses Phase: the phase during which the lining is shed; that is, the days that the woman menstruates.
Five days in average.
Occurs during the early days of the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle when progesterone, FSH, and LH levels are low .
Easy concepts
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The image shows the uterine cycle phases.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-The Uterine (Menstrual) Cycle  
Proliferative Phase: 
Starts once menstrual flow ceases.
The endometrium begins to proliferate again, marking the beginning of the proliferative phase
It occurs when the tertiary follicles begin to produce increased amounts of estrogen.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The image shows the uterine cycle phases.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-The Uterine (Menstrual) Cycle  
Proliferative Phase: 
Rising estrogen concentrations stimulate the endometrial lining to rebuild.
The elevated estrogen levels stimulates the LH surge that will trigger ovulation. 
In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, ovulation occurs on day 14. 
Ovulation marks the end of the proliferative phase as well as the end of the follicular phase.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The image shows the uterine cycle phases.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-The Uterine (Menstrual) Cycle  
Secretory phase
In the ovary, and after ovulation, corpus luteum produce progesterone.
In the uterus, this marks the beginning of secretory phase of the menstrual cycle.
The endometrial lining prepares for implantation 
The endometrial glands secrete a fluid rich in glycogen which will nourish cells of the fertilized egg. 
At the same time, the spiral arteries develop to provide blood to the thickened functional layer.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The image shows the uterine cycle phases.
occurrences.slide_text:
6-The Uterine (Menstrual) Cycle  
Secretory phase
If no pregnancy occurs within approximately 10 to 12 days, the corpus luteum will degrade into the corpus albicans. 
Levels of both estrogen and progesterone will fall, and the endometrium will grow thinner. 
The endometrial tissue will die, resulting in menses—or the first day of the next cycle.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top panel of this image shows the stages in the follicular phase and how one follicle is selected at the end of this phase. The middle part of this image shows the ovarian cycle phases and the uterine cycle phases. The bottom panel shows the levels of different hormones as a function of time.
occurrences.slide_text:
The Ovarian and Uterine Cycles
Both cycles happening at the same time at two different locations.
Different hormones play different roles in each location.
Main hormones are LH, FSH, Estrogen and Progesterone. 
Several negative and positive feedback loops regulate the production of these hormones.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top part of this image shows the ovarian cycle phases and the uterine cycle phases. The bottom panel shows the levels of different hormones as a function of time.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Effects of Hormones
FSH and LH: 
Both hormones levels peak just prior to ovulation. 
During follicular phase they stimulate follicles to grow.
During ovulation: promote one of them to release the egg.
During luteal phase, LH stimulates formation of corpus luteum and therefore promote progesterone production
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top part of this image shows the ovarian cycle phases and the uterine cycle phases. The bottom panel shows the levels of different hormones as a function of time.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Effects of Hormones
Estrogen: 
Promote oogenesis and follicle growth in ovary
Exert anabolic effect on female reproductive tract
Support rapid short-lived growth spurts at puberty
Induce secondary sex characteristics
Growth of breasts
Increased deposit of subcutaneous fat (hips and breasts)
Widening and lightening of pelvis
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The top part of this image shows the ovarian cycle phases and the uterine cycle phases. The bottom panel shows the levels of different hormones as a function of time.
occurrences.slide_text:
Progesterone:
Works with estrogen to establish and regulate uterine cycle
Promotes changes in cervical mucus
Prevent developing more than one oocyte per ovarian cycle.
Effects of placental progesterone during pregnancy
Inhibits uterine motility
Helps prepare breasts for lactation
3-Effects of Hormones
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This multipart diagram shows the cross section of the penis. The top left panel shows the lateral view of the flaccid penis and the top right panel shows the transverse view.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Penis
Each of the two larger lateral chambers is called a corpus cavernosum. Together, these make up the bulk of the penis.
The corpus spongiosum is a smaller chamber that surrounds the spongy urethra.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This multipart diagram shows the cross section of the penis. The top left panel shows the lateral view of the flaccid penis and the top right panel shows the transverse view.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-The Penis
The end of the penis, called the glans penis, has a high concentration of nerve endings, resulting in very sensitive skin that influences the likelihood of ejaculation. 
The skin from the shaft extends down over the glans and forms a collar called the prepuce (or foreskin). Removed by circumcision, for religious or social or medical reasons.
Removing it reduces the risk of HIV infections
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This multipart diagram shows the cross section of the penis. The left panel shows the lateral view of the erect penis and the bottom right panel shows the transverse view.
occurrences.slide_text:
4-The Penis
Erections are the result of vasocongestion, or enlargement of the tissues because of more arterial blood flowing into the penis than is leaving in the veins.
During sexual arousal, nitric oxide (NO) is released from nerve endings near blood vessels within the corpora cavernosa and spongiosum.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This multipart diagram shows the cross section of the penis. The left panel shows the lateral view of the erect penis and the bottom right panel shows the transverse view.
occurrences.slide_text:
5-The Penis
Release of NO results in relaxation of the smooth muscles that surround the penile arteries, causing them to dilate. 
This dilation increases the amount of blood that can enter the penis. 
Blood fills the erectile chambers.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view and the bottom panel shows the anterior view.
occurrences.slide_text:
Vagina
muscular canal (approximately 10 cm long) that serves as the entrance to the reproductive tract.
It also serves as the exit from the uterus during menses and childbirth.
the superior portion of the vagina—called the fornix—meets the uterine cervix.
Easy concepts

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the ovary.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Ovaries
Easy concepts
Oocytes develop within the outer layer of this stroma, each surrounded by supporting cells. 
This grouping of an oocyte and its supporting cells is called a follicle.
The development of an oocyte happens through what is known as ovarian cycle.
By Kimanh Nguyen - https://mla-lima.wikispaces.com/Anatomy+of+the+Ovaries?responseToken=01fcd85f07c85da7489dd7e2a01e82bf0, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=71030506
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: The panel shows the lateral view of the ovary.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Ovarian Cycle
A set of changes in a female’s oocytes and ovarian follicles.
Roughly 28-day cycle.
Two phases: 
Follicular phase: includes oogenesis (the production of female gametes) and folliculogenesis (the growth and development of ovarian follicles); both happening at the same time.
Luteal phase: the post-ovulatory phase
By Kimanh Nguyen - https://mla-lima.wikispaces.com/Anatomy+of+the+Ovaries?responseToken=01fcd85f07c85da7489dd7e2a01e82bf0, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=71030506
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This multipart figure shows how follicles are generated. The panel shows the first three stages of folliculogenesis. In each stage, the major cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-Follicular phase: Folliculogenesis
Primordial follicles are present in newborn females and have only a single flat layer of support cells.
After puberty, a few primordial follicles will develop into primary follicles and later a secondary follicle. 
Secondary follicle contains more than one layer of supporting cells
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This multipart figure shows how follicles are generated. The panel shows the last three stages of folliculogenesis. In each stage, the major cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
3-Follicular phase: Folliculogenesis
Secondary follicle will keep growing into a tertiary follicle. 
Contains antrum which holds follicular fluid.
Several follicles reach the tertiary stage at the same time, and most of these will undergo death.
One tertiary follicle will continue to grow and develop until ovulation
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: . The panel shows the first three stages of folliculogenesis. In each stage, the major cell types are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-Luteal phase
The follicle that released its oocyte turns into a new endocrine structure called the corpus luteum, a term meaning “yellowish body”.
In case of pregnancy, corpus luteum will release progesterone.  
Sustained progesterone levels are important in maintain pregnancy.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows the anatomy of the breast. The left panel shows the front view and the right panel shows the side view. The main parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
1-The Breasts
Considered accessory organs of the female reproductive system.
The function of the breasts is to supply milk to an infant in a process called lactation.
The external features of the breast include a nipple surrounded by a pigmented areola
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.

occurrences.alt: This figure shows  the side view of the breast. The left panel shows the front view and the right panel shows the side view. The main parts are labeled.
occurrences.slide_text:
2-The Breasts
Breast milk is produced by the mammary glands.
Milk-secreting cells cluster in structures called alveoli. Several alveoli are grouped in lobule that surrounded by fat tissue.
Milk exits the lobule through lactiferous ducts which extend to a lactiferous sinus. 
15 to 20 lactiferous ducts open on the surface of the nipple.
occurrences.credit: Lecture adaptation: Ahmed Katsha, Raritan Valley Community College; OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY 4.0. See original slide credit for exceptions.
